speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ANNUAL REPORT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated only a few moments ago that I was intending to make a statement in the House with reference to the annual report of the Farm Credit Corporation. The document, upon study, really contains no surprises for those who have been following agricultural events over the last five or 10 years. The Farm Credit Corporation is reporting major losses again this year. It is important for Canadians to understand how the
Farm Credit Corporation got into this situation in the first place and it is important as well to understand how this Government intends to bring the Farm Credit Corporation back onto sound financial footings.
In the 1970s, the so-called experts made a number of predictions that affected, and affected very seriously, many conventional or traditional lending institutions, and they also made some predictions that had a very severe impact especially on the Farm Credit Corporation. The so-called experts indicated and sent out messages to the effect that interest rates would remain stable. They said that energy costs would remain stable. They said that the inflation rate would remain stable. They said that we would be going through a time, now in the mid-eighties and beyond, of world shortages in food supply. They also said that we would be going through a period of time in our history when commodity prices would be reaching alltime high levels. Obviously, they were wrong on all accounts.
At that time, farmers were encouraged to borrow money to buy land and to expand their operations. By the mid-1970s, the Farm Credit Corporation could not supply credit to meet the demands. In 1975, the Farm Credit Corporation Act was revised to provide 100 per cent of the market value on security of the collateral for the loan.
Again, between 1972 and 1983, loan limits were increased five times to keep up with the inflation of the farm asset value. The lending decisions were made on market expectations that just did not materialize. The widely available credit resulted in heavy borrowing and the farm debt shot up from $4.6 billion in 1971 to $18.6 billion in 1981.
Then in the early 1980s, interest rates shot up. In fact, they increased by about 12 per cent to reach record highs of some 22 per cent or 23 per cent. For farmers, each percentage point represents an additional cost of about $150 million. That increase in interest rates of 12 per cent was a direct input cost to Canadian farmers of nearly $2 billion.
At the same time, commodity prices dropped, especially for grains. Incomes dropped and so did farm asset values drop by nearly $20 billion. Farmers with high debt loads were crippled and the Farm Credit Corporation became a lender of last resort. The Farm Credit Corporation found itself serving clients who owed more than the sale of their land could possibly recover.

July 21, 1988
Statements by Ministers
[DOT] (mo)
Today we see the result of all those factors. Some 96 per cent of all FCC arrears today relate to those loans made prior to 1984. That was a direct result of the conditions during that period of time, and last year the FCC lost $511.8 million.
This Government has made it a priority to restore order to FCC policies and put the corporation back on its feet. These measures include a moratorium on foreclosures in 1984 and 1985; an $80 million interest rate reduction program in 1985; a shared risk mortgage introduced in 1985; farm debt review legislation was passed; farm debt review boards were established. As a matter of interest, a recent survey showed that 74 per cent of those who have used the boards are satisfied with the process. As well, we put in place the Canadian Rural Transition Program and also amended and enhanced the Farm Improvements Loans Act.
Last December, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that this Government would provide $100 million to help cover FCC losses. More assistance was given to the corporation to allow it to participate fully in the farm debt review process. We put in new managers at the corporation and gave them the responsibility and the challenge of developing a recovery plan. Today, I am announcing that this Government will contribute another $400 million as part of that recovery plan. We will be injecting more money into FCC over the next three years.
The message we are sending out today on behalf of the Government is the fact that the FCC is here and here to stay. This Government stands firmly behind the corporation and is helping to solve its financial problems. This new money will ensure that FCC continues to serve farmers, and a healthier corporation means better service to farmers.
The corporation's role has also been clarified. Its primary job is to provide long-term mortgage credit to Canadian farmers on a break-even basis. It will be an alternative source of credit to average risk farmers, as well as those who represent a marginally higher risk but who have significant potential for commercial viability. These measures will ensure that our farmers have a reliable source of long-term credit when they need it, and that future FCC clients will not be penalized by past corporate losses. These measures also ensure that the corporation will be able to offer competitive interest rates.
Today's financial recovery plan is only the latest evidence of this Government's commitment to Canadian agriculture. In the last four years we undertook initiatives worth nearly $10 billion to our agri-food industry. We made record payments under the Special Canadian Grains Program, stabilization programs, drought assistance programs, and the list goes on. Our record on agriculture is second to none. We stand squarely behind Canadian farmers. We are determined to put the Farm Credit Corporation on a financially sound basis. We will
ensure that it continues to provide long-term credit to Canadian farmers.
Some Hon. Mlembers: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been said before that never has so much been said about so little, the "so little" being of course the action of the Government in its assistance to agriculture.
The Government today prides itself on having bailed out the Farm Credit Corporation after it allowed it to go broke to start with. The Tories applaud the fact that the Government has, a year after the FCC was technically broke, bailed it out and put it back on the footing on which it should have been all along. We are supposed to be very grateful for this.
I was thinking this morning that the Government was going to come into this House and tell us about a massive program of assistance for farmers. I thought the announcement that the Minister was going to make on the FCC would include such things as that the corporation's current losses would be supported by the Government on a long-term basis. I thought the Government would say the FCC would play a brand new and innovative role in the development of financial services for farmers. I hoped to hear the Government would recognize the need for a policy role for the FCC and would commit itself to compensate the corporation for the losses it incurs while developing these policies. I was hoping to hear the Minister tell us today that the FCC would establish a brand new set of programs for beginning farmers and set standards for management skills of beginning farmers, that it would recycle FCC properties and recycle them for beginning farmers. Those are the kinds of things I was hoping to hear the Minister say this morning, but I did not hear any of them.
I was hoping to hear as well that the federal Government was finally going to bail out the FCC from the poor condition it allowed it to get into. Of course I was hoping that. That is the least the Government could do. As usual the Government did the very least it could have done.
I listened with great attention and read the Minister's speech, and I thank him for having the courtesy to provide me with a copy some minutes ago. I was wondering whether it would be delivered by the Minister. I will just refresh your memory on what the Minister just said. He said:
This Government has made it a priority to restore order to FCC policies-
Order? It allowed the FCC to go broke! Is that what you call order? It has to be Tory order but it is not logical order and it is certainly not farm order. Farmers do not run their businesses that way.
The Government says it initiated a number of things such as a moratorium on farm foreclosures. The Government says it initiated farm debt review measures and so on. I am glad to see the Minister listened to some of the suggestions made by Ralph Ferguson and others in the past.

If one does not do that, then it is plagiarism. We would not want to accuse the Minister of that.
One of the most important things 1 read in this statement today is this very short sentence:
FCC is here to stay.
That is an important statement. It is probably more important than anything else in the Minister's speech this morning. That statement is symbolically important for all farmers. It is my hope that the Government and the Minister mean what they say in that statement. It means the FCC has to exist as something other than a name. An organization which is broke now and has been broke for almost a year is not exactly something that looks as though it were here to stay.
I urge the Minister not only to provide the funding today which will satisfy the FCC for the short term because it has this huge backlog of cases to deal with but, more important, to make a commitment that the Government, and any future Government, will not allow the FCC to go broke as the Minister and his Government have done.
I know that the time afforded to us is very limited. That is unfortunate because I could go on and on talking about agriculture and the sad record of the Government in supporting agriculture. The Government has failed to convince its friend, the United States of America with whom it is trying to sign a trade deal, to stop this war on subsidies which has caused the prices of agricultural commodities to go down so much and which has caused so many of the problems we have today. The Government has failed miserably in that regard.
We must remember as well that the excess farm debt at the present in this country is $22 billion. There is $22 billion of excess debt which farmers will never be able to handle. As a matter of fact, the Standing Committee on Agriculture will be reporting on that issue and making a number of recommendations which I cannot reveal, obviously, because they have not yet been reported to the House and I, of course, would never leak the contents of a committee report.
The Minister said, "Our record on agriculture is second to none". What he should have said is, "Our record on agriculture is none to second".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is amazing how an impending election can bring a tottering Government out of the doldrums and get it to make decisions, statements, announcements of funds which are suddenly available for a variety of reasons-which funds were probably going to be available anyway in some cases-or the re-
Statements by Ministers
announcement of funds that have already been announced and put in place.
Much of the Minister's statement dealt with the history of the Farm Credit Corporation. History is important to know and to learn from. However, it has little value to the credit-starved farmers looking for assistance. The deficit situation of the Farm Credit Corporation is a direct result of decisions made by the previous Government. That Government decided to find money on the market rather than use the money available through the Government.
The Minister indicated that he was going to announce a recovery plan, but failed to do so. The deficit of the Farm Credit Corporation was allowed to grow and the corporation almost reached the situation of being no longer viable. A bailout was necessary. Last December, $100 million was announced and the $400 million announced today covers part of the deficit, but it does not put the Farm Credit Corporation into a position where it can return to the role for which it was originally established. That is something the Minister will have to do before the effect of this money will be felt by the farmers.
There are thousands of farmers in very difficult straits. This so-called recovery plan will give them no more hope of survival. There are a couple of things which this recovery plan could have done which it did not do. For instance, it made no attempt to shield the farmers from high interest rates. The Government has been supporting the increase in interest rates by a Bank of Canada policy which is already affecting the survival of farmers who require credit to continue operating. Interest rates are on the rise to such an extent that they are a factor in the elimination of more farmers each year. This so-called recovery plan contains no protection for farmers in that regard.
It failed to announce the quality or quantity of funds which would be available for lending to farmers in the future. The fact that there are thousands of farmers who need credit now and need a plan to keep them on the farms is not going to be affected by the putting into place of enough money to bring the Farm Credit Corporation out of a deficit position.
Third, as long as the Farm Credit Corporation operates as a bank it will continue to abandon the thousands of farmers who need action for their survival. As long as the Farm Credit Corporation continues to be just another bank it will not help those farmers.
In the past the Farm Credit Corporation has been a very important factor in agriculture, and it can be so again. It must be so again. However, the recovery plan which the Minister suggests he is putting in place, which I suppose could be called a non-recovery plan, will not do much toward establishing a comprehensive structure which would allow farmers to survive, farmers getting into agriculture, to have a source of funds without having to go to the banks and take the kinds of risks which were taken in the past, and to allow able farmers to continue in their present structure.

July 21, 1988
Committee Reports
I am glad that the Farm Credit Corporation is going to be able to eliminate part of its deficit. However, we need answers about how the Farm Credit Corporation will operate relative to farmers in the future. Those are the kinds of answers the Minister did not give in his statement.
I hope the Minister will follow through on the position he has taken and give us, in the very near future, a comprehensive plan for the Farm Credit Corporation so that farmers will have some security about the availability of credit and the price they will have to pay for that credit.

Mr. Speaker, on a morning when there is controversy in Parliament and the country about whether a specific question such as free trade ought to be submitted to a general election or to the other place, the Senate, I am happy to be able to introduce for first reading a Bill that would point to a third way. The national referendum and plebiscite Act, or La loi Canadienne sur les referendums et plebiscites, is a complete code providing for the holding of referendums and plebiscites in Canada.
This Bill is certified in order, seconded by my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). It runs to some 363 pages and attempts to deal in every respect, whether with broadcasting, fairness of publicity, spending limits, and all of the issues that are important to fair and unsullied expression of direct public opinion.
In my view, it is high time that we had such a statute that would give that third option for direct expression of popular opinion. I am happy to bring this Bill before the House this morning for first reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak on the tax reform Bill today and to explain some of the benefits of the Government's tax reform legislation. All Canadians benefit from tax reform, either from having their own taxes lowered or through the increased economic activity that will flow from an improved, more efficient and more equitable tax system.
Previous speakers in this debate have examined various aspects of tax reform. As both a member of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs and as Chairman of the government caucus Health and Welfare Committee, I would like to look at how our comprehensive tax reform package provides significant benefits to Canadian families. Most important, tax reform means that Canadians will pay lower taxes this year than they did in 1987. Tax reform will reduce personal income tax for eight out of 10 Canadian households and for almost nine out of 10 Canadians over the age of 65. In other words, about 9.7 million households will enjoy an average tax cut of almost $500.
As well, Canadians will generally find their provincial income taxes reduced in the nine provinces that have tax collection agreements with the federal Government. Quebec has also made a number of changes to allow residents of that province to benefit from our tax reform measures. I said that Canadians will "generally find their provincial income taxes reduced'' because there is one province where the provincial Treasurer has taken some action to pre-empt the tax benefits that should be flowing to the residents of that province. I refer, of course, to the Finance Minister, Mr. Nixon, of Ontario, who introduced increases in taxes to take away the benefits that
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
would flow to families in Ontario before they could be received.
Most individuals are already benefiting from higher take-home pay. As of July 1, most pay cheques are larger, reflecting the reduction in taxes as a result of tax reform. Further adjustments in taxes, of course, will occur at year end. Tax reform will also mean a fairer tax system. The key to improving the fairness of the system under tax reform is replacing a number of the old system's exemptions and deductions with tax credits.
Tax credits are fairer because they directly reduce tax payable. This means that a tax credit is worth the same to all Canadians regardless of their level of income. By contrast, under the old system, exemptions were of greater value to people with higher incomes because they reduced the amount of income subject to tax at the higher tax rates.
As a result of converting exemptions to credits, approximately 850,000 lower-income Canadians will have their federal personal income tax reduced to zero. Converting exemptions to credits will provide important financial benefits to Canadian families in a variety of ways. For instance, under tax reform, the married exemption will be converted to a credit. This will benefit many households where the second spouse has a modest income from part-time work or small investments. Currently, the married exemption is reduced by one dollar for every dollar of net income earned by a spouse above a threshold. As a result, a part of the earnings of the lower-income spouse are effectively taxed at the rate applicable to the higher-income spouse.
With tax reform, this inequity will no longer exist. The first $27,500 of income earned by the low-income spouse will be subject to tax at the federal rate of 17 per cent. The conversion of the married exemption to a tax credit thus removes the tax penalty that can now discourage a second income earner from entering the labour force. The new married or equivalent to married credit of $850 represents a significant increase over the old exemption. Indeed, for most Canadians, the new credit is equivalent to an exemption of $5,000 or $1,260 more than the old exemption would have been worth this year.
More than two million lower-income families will benefit from the higher refundable sales tax credit, the increase to $70 from $50 for adults and $35 from $25 for children. The family net income threshold at which the credit begins to be reduced has been raised by $1,000 to $16,000. These measures will protect lower-income Canadians from the impact of interim changes to the federal sales tax as part of the first stage of tax reform.
The refundable sales tax credit will be significantly enriched and extended to more Canadians in stage two of tax reform when the current federal sales tax will be replaced with a new sales tax. Many families, and single Canadians, will also benefit from the changed treatment of education expenses. The current education expense deduction will become a tax credit

Income Tax Act and Related Acts
of $10 per month. In addition, the deductions for tuition fees will be replaced by a tax credit of 17 per cent of post-secondary tuition fees. Quite importantly, the unused portion of the first $600 of these credits can be transferred to a supporting parent, spouse or grandparent. This is an important new feature. Before tax reform tuition fees could only be claimed by the student, even when the student did not have sufficient income to benefit from the use of the exemption.
Under tax reform the income level at which families start paying tax will rise. The increased value of personal tax credits raises the tax thresholds. That is the main reason that the 850,000 lower-income Canadians I mentioned earlier will have their income tax cut to zero.
For example, this year a couple with one earner and with two children will not pay any federal income tax until their income reaches $18,890. This compares with a threshold before tax reform of $16,770.
After presenting the original White Paper proposals the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) consulted with Canadians and gave the tax reform proposals to the Finance Committee which made a number of recommendations for improvements. Many of these improvements increased benefits for families with children.
For example, the refundable child tax credit was increased to $559 as of January 1 of this year. The dependent child credit, which replaces the old exemption, was set at $65 per child. However, for the third and subsequent children the tax credit was doubled to $130. The credits were also made available for the full year in which the child turns 18. A dependent child is now able to earn as much as $2,500 before the credit begins to be phased out.
While I have been dwelling this morning on benefits to families, it is fair to point out that a number of these increases were recommended by the Finance Committee and, indeed, the means to pay for them was also recommended by the Finance Committee in its report. The money has come from imposing effective taxes, alternative minimum taxes, for the first time on our large financial institutions. In this way banks, trust companies, life insurance companies, property and casualty insurance companies and real estate companies, which effectively for the large part have been paying no taxes whatsoever on their profits for the last 10 years, will indeed pay taxes under tax reform. By and large these taxes are being used to finance these family benefit tax credits to which I have been referring.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) also announced the Government's new national strategy on child care last December. By doubling the maximum child care expense deduction to $4,000 for each child who is six years old and under, and by introducing a supplement to the refundable child tax credit for those who do not have receipted child care expenses, we have increased substantially the level of tax assistance for parents.
Many families will also benefit from the improvements we have made to a number of the old deductions. The new
medical expense credit will provide similar tax relief to all taxpayers with uninsured medical expenses. The charitable donations credit improves the tax incentive for the vast majority of Canadians to make larger donations. The improved disability credit not only is fairer to people at all income levels, it also increases tax assistance for the majority in the 17 per cent bracket. Greater fairness is being achieved by converting the deductions for the CPP/QPP contributions and UI premiums into credits of 17 per cent.
When one combines our tax reform measures with the improvements in tax assistance announced as part of the child care policy, it is clear that this Government is committed to improving the well-being of Canadian families.
If Members opposite share the Government's commitment to the Canadian family, they can show their support by voting in favour of this Bill to implement our tax reform proposals.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask about fairness and therefore will ask a rather technical question of my friend who is also a member of the Finance Committee. I ask this question because I think it is a serious issue which is difficult to ventilate in the House of Commons.
In the House of Commons we have been talking about the unfairness of Conservative tax reform and the fact that while taxes on many families are down from last year, according to the tax reform, they are up from 1984. The only people who have tax cuts from 1984 under Tory tax reform are people earning over $100,000 per year.
Because of the fact that the Hon. Member and I worked together on this matter I would like to remind him of the report of the committee with respect to the issue of the proposed anti-avoidance rule. The Hon. Member for Scarborough will recall that the committee rejected the Government's proposed new anti-avoidance rules. It rejected them because of the feeling that we would be into a period of six, seven or eight years of turmoil before the courts began to define more precisely what the new anti-avoidance provisions meant. There was a feeling, which I believe the Hon. Member shared, that a large part of the problem was not the legislation but the lack of aggressiveness of the Department of National Revenue and, perhaps, the Ministry of Finance in actually pursuing avoidance transactions under the present law. We felt that the present law could be changed modestly in order to make it more effective.
I wonder if the Hon. Member can comment on the Government's determination to ignore the advice of the elected representatives, which came from all Parties, and which was offered not just by the New Democratic members or by the Liberal members of the committee but by the Progressive Conservative members as well. Can the Hon. Member comment on the failure of the Government to look seriously at the proposed anti-avoidance provision which the committee recommended and which was based, if I recall correctly, on submissions which we had from experts such as the Bar Association and chartered accountants?
July 21, 1988

The Hon. Member will recall the fact that, after the Ways and Means Motion which contained the draft legislation was made public in April, the joint committee of the bar and of the chartered accountants came back before the committee and once again told us categorically, and 1 think constructively, that it thought that the proposed legislation was wrong. It said that it would create enormous problems and that, far from stopping anti-avoidance devices and dodges being used by different companies, speculators and people in the stock market, in fact it would create more problems than it would solve.
I recognize that many of the people who are active in the tax committee of the bar and of the accounting profession are some of the people who are advising private plans on these avoidance schemes. However, in listening to the testimony I was convinced that they were, nonetheless, and regardless of a potential conflict of interest, not trying to leave Parliament and the Government boxed in but that they were speaking to loopholes and running room which had been created for them by a lack of aggressive action and enforcement.
Will the Hon. Member comment on how he can support this Bill when in this particular area which, in the end, is so offensive to average Canadians, the Government, in an excess of zeal, has created probably a weaker instrument than it could have had with the existing legislation had it been reinforced?

The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) has raised two points. The first point he raised had to do with the level of taxes paid under tax reform. The second point had to do not with anything 1 said but with matters we heard in the committee with respect to the antiavoidance rules in the tax legislation. I will deal with both points separately.
With respect to the level of taxes which will be paid, I think that the Hon. Member has arrived at a false conclusion. His conclusion is false, and demonstrably false, as a result of the details which were provided to the Finance Committee. It is false in respect to two separate areas.
First, he indicates that in general taxpayers earning over $100,000 will pay less tax under the new system than under the old system. I categorically reject this. Indeed, all the evidence presented to the Finance Committee also rejects the same assertion. The Hon. Member rather conveniently ignores the large number of tax references which have been closed out which were largely utilized by these people making over $100,000. Indeed, the distribution of taxes provided with the tax reform package indicates that, of the 20 per cent of Canadians who will pay higher taxes, and as I recall it will average in excess of $500 a year more in taxes, it is concentrated largely with those earning $100,000 a year as a result of the much fairer and systematic elimination of loopholes and curtailment of tax preferences.
Second, the Hon. Member makes the sweeping assertion that Canadians will pay more taxes as a result of what I
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
believe is a misinterpretation of figures. I certainly would not want to suggest it was a deliberate misinterpretation. However, one of the things I have noticed is that the Hon. Member has a tendency to look at the trend in personal income taxes. Since that trend has been going up over the four years, he has come to the conclusion that the level of taxes has gone up significantly over the four years including tax reform.
In his calculations the Hon. Member made the significant omission of looking at the increased number of people who are participating in the workplace as a result of the very large drop in the unemployment rate that has taken place under this Government.
Therefore, one cannot look at the trend in personal income tax collections and divide it by the population and state that the average taxpayer is paying more. One has to look at the number of people who are working and paying taxes rather than collecting unemployment insurance or welfare.
With respect to the second point of the Hon. Member, the general anti-avoidance rules in the legislation, in part I agree with the Hon. Member. Following the tabling of the draft legislation, I would agree with him that the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants did appear before the committee and did indicate that they had serious reservations about-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the speech of my hon. colleague on tax reform. It was an interesting speech, but I think the Hon. Member missed the point on a number of occasions in describing exactly what has happened under the so-called tax reform of the Conservative Government. It is now well known that while the tax system has been changed rather than reformed, it has been somewhat deformed. If the tax system was unjust before the Conservatives examined it, it is now more unfair; if it was discriminatory against the poor, it is now more than ever discriminatory against the poor; if it advantaged the wealthy, it now more than ever advantages the wealthy; if it was a complicated system before, it is more complicated now.

July 21, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
The best reference that I have read relating to the Conservative Government's view of tax reform is "Robin Elood in reverse". Rather than take from the rich and give to the poor, tax reform for the Conservatives is take from the poor and give to the rich. Very clearly, the beneficiaries of the tax reform of the Conservative Government are those Canadians who are the wealthiest Canadians. Once again, the rest of Canadian society has been hammered and hosed through this tax reform package so that more than ever they are paying more taxes now than when the Conservative Government took office.
If one totalled all the tax increases that the average Canadian family has experienced under the Conservative Government, for example, income tax increases, gasoline tax increases, and sales tax increases of one type or another, it would be found that, compared to September, 1984, in September, 1988, the average Canadian family will be paying $1,000 more in federal taxes under the Mulroney Government. That is an absolute tragedy. In all the communities of Canada it means that that $1,000 per family is not circulating in the community from business to business and person to person to keep the local economy going.
There are tens of thousands of people in our country who need shelter or affordable homes. The only shelter the Conservative Government is involved with is sheltering taxes for the various wealthy Canadians. "Tax shelter", is what the Government means when it talks about "shelter". There are dozens of tax shelters technically designed to assist the Canadian economy, but in reality they result in a handful of rich people becoming richer.
Together with a number of my colleagues in the New Democratic caucus I have the privilege to work on Tax Probe 1986 which began in 1986. For two years we travelled the country and talked to tax experts on the East Coast, in central Canada, on the Prairies, on the West Coast, and up into the North. We talked to every conceivable person we could find who was interested in talking about how to reform the tax system. We asked the questions: "As a tax expert, what tax loophole is a good one?" "As Mr. and Mrs. Tax Expert, which tax loophole would you say that Canada is getting good value for?" "If it costs the taxpayers of Canada $500 million of lost taxes, how much do we gain from that in addition to the tax loss?" There was not one single tax accountant, tax lawyer, or tax adviser who was prepared to stand up and say that a certain tax loophole is good for Canada. Certain tax loopholes are good for some people or a handful of investors, but when asked if they were good for Canada, not a single expert was prepared to say they were.
I am not prepared to say that there is not a good tax loophole, but after two years of searching out the nooks and crannies of the country and examining page by page the
complicated tax Act, we could not find a single tax loophole that made economic financial sense.
How can one summarize the Conservative view of tax reform? At the top of the list is this puzzling question that has been put to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) so many times that it has become a boring question. The question is: "Under your tax reform system, how is it that 60,000 profitable corporations do not pay a single penny in income tax?" Presumably the Minister of Finance is proud of what he has done to the tax system to improve it, but he allows 60,000 profitable companies to pay not a single penny in income tax. That is to say nothing of the thousands of companies that might pay $10 or $50 in income tax a year, but those 60,000 profitable corporations do not even pay five cents.
They are not small companies, or companies that we call the "Mom and Pop Shops" of Canada. In some years they are companies such as the Royal Bank of Canada. In other years it will be the Bank of Montreal, Cadillac-Fairview, General Motors, or Shell Oil. There are 60,000 corporations that do not pay anything.
We have said that it is time that that changes, that it is time that we start building some fairness into our tax system. If we are going to build fairness, it means that those corporations that are very profitable should be paying their fair share. They should not be paying more than their fair share but just their fair share. I noticed that in the United States, back in 1986, the President introduced a tax law that requires every profitable company in the United States to pay at least a minimum corporate tax of 20 per cent. That was accepted in the United States as fair and reasonable. That was accepted by large, small and medium-sized corporations as the decent thing to do, so that they would be able to pay their fair share. After all, their profits and so on were coming from a country and an economy where they obviously were benefiting, and they felt that 20 per cent minimum was a fair corporate tax.
Does our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) do the same thing in Canada? Unfortunately not. He is not prepared even to touch that aspect of our tax system. I say that that is wrong, unjust, unfair and discriminatory, particularly against the people of Canada and against the small business sector of Canada.
As our well-known friend, John Bulloch, who heads the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, has indicated, our tax system is discriminatory against the small and medium-sized business in Canada. They pay their fair share and they pay what is a reasonable amount of tax, in some cases too much. They have to pay more than they should, because the large profitable corporation in some cases pays zero. We are saying that that is reflective of an unfair tax system.
July 21, 1988

Now, one can go on and speak on the personal side of the tax system. Under tax reform, the stockbroker in downtown Toronto who might make $200,000 a year will save $15,000 under Mr. Wilson's tax reform. He will save $15,000 because his rates have gone down, and yet, there are hundreds of thousands of people whose incomes rank below the poverty line who still pay income tax.
Young families struggling to get established, working hard, receiving a very modest income, pay income tax, pay $50, $100, and yet tax reform means that the stockbroker who makes $200,000 is going to save $15,000 this year on his or her income tax. That is the kind of unfairness that is perpetuated by this tax reform picture.
My dad is nearly 83 years old. He worked all of his life, saved modestly so that he could have a decent pension. He has to pay taxes on a small savings account. My dad, 83 years old, pays more income tax in some years than the Royal Bank of Canada. My dad pays more taxes in some years than Shell Oil. That is wrong. Who could sit here and say that this is a good system, that this is a fair system? My dad does not feel that way.
The tax returns that most of us have tried to fill out in the last few months, in that annual ritual where we sit awake late at night, night after night, with dictionaries and calculators and sheets of paper, trying to figure out what our tax bill should be that year, is an ordeal. I look forward to it in most years with some terror. I know that as simplistic as it seems to be, it inevitably ends up with weeks and weeks of agonizing. You finally sit down at your table and pull it all together and send it in, and it always comes back changed. They always change it. The tax minions look over your return and find that you have been a few cents out here and there, or you missed a space there, and you get a redone return mailed back.
Fifty-one per cent of Canadians cannot fill out their own tax returns; they have to pay somebody to do it. Fifty-one per cent of tax filers have to go to a third party to fill out their tax returns. Well, that is not right. It is not necessary. Under tax reform we have seen the system complicated even further.
Some members of the Finance Committee are here today. They will remember that the Finance Committee examined a simplified tax return. We studied this for some months. We looked at what other countries do, and we found that for the majority of Canadians a single-page tax return would be all that is necessary. About 10 lines, that is all that is required. With that, about 70 per cent of Canadians would not have to look forward to this annual tax return horror show every spring.
Did the Government introduce that? No, it did not. There are pages and pages of tax returns that have to be filled out now by the average Canadian. Well, you will look through the lists and lists and you will ask yourself what this tax reform has done to us. Is it Robin Hood in reverse? Is it tax shelters not for the homeless but for the wealthy? Is it tax reform not for the needy but for the greedy? Those people that have are
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
going to get more. The average family in this country is paying an extra $1,000 in federal taxes.
Now, there are some changes. I would like to look through a list that we have compiled as to what we think should be done in terms of our tax system. At the top of the list would obviously be a tax system with a more simplified return so that Canadians would not have to agonize each spring while they fill out their tax return, with some exceptions. Obviously, if you have a complicated investment portfolio you will have to go to some pains to fill out that tax return. But for the average working Canadian man and woman, that is not necessary.
We would also like to see the structure of our tax rates examined and that a higher top rate be imposed. After all, is it not reasonable to expect that someone who makes a great deal of money should pay at a higher tax rate than someone who is making money that classifies him or her as living below the poverty line? In other words, the more you make the more you should contribute to the country where you make that money.
We are also concerned about what is taxed. I think a lot of people assume that wherever you make your money you pay the same tax. That is not the case. If you make your money speculating in property or in gold stocks or whatever, you do not pay the same tax as someone who is working in an office or a factory or a mine or a mill. We classify that kind of money differently. We say that you do not have to pay on all of that income. As a matter of fact, up to a certain level you do not have to pay any tax at all. So if you speculate on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange and you make good money on an annual basis, you do not have to pay any tax on that, no tax whatsoever. Why not? You have a capital gains allowance of up to $100,000. If you do, you only pay tax on half of the capital gains, not on a dollar.
What I am saying is that, depending on how you make your income, you pay different kinds of taxes. That is not fair. We say that capital gains ought to be exempt for people running small businesses or are family farmers, because that is the way that they provide for their retirements and so on, but not generally speaking. A buck should be a buck. That is going back to the Carter Commission many years ago. The suggestion at that time was that if we were going to have tax we should tax people on a buck being a buck, and not a buck being 50 cents for some people.
I think that all Members of Parliament would agree that the family farm has to be protected because that is the way people provide for their retirement years, and similarly the family business. I am not talking about General Motors in this case; I am talking about people you see as you walk up and down the main streets of Canada, running their independent businesses.
There are other changes that we have suggested. We are very concerned, in regard to the new tax being planned called the national federal sales tax, about the decision by the Government to impose now a sales tax on everything, every business transaction.

July 21, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts

speechtext: Even the haircuts.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS

When you get a haircut, as my hon. friend from Vanier reminds me, you will pay a new Mulroney sales tax. When you go out and buy a new shirt, when you have your laundry done, when you go to the movies, when you fill out your will, no matter what you do, every single business transaction in this country, large or small, will be taxed.
For the first time in history we are going to have a federal sales tax. It might be called something different, it might be called a value-added tax, it might be called a business transfer tax, it might be called a national sales tax, but whatever it is called it will be a national sales tax that will be imposed on every man, woman and child in this country.
My friend from Fraser Valley is asking what it will replace. I will tell you. We do not pay a national sales tax now when we go to the movies. We do not pay a national sales tax now when we have a will made. We do not pay a national sales tax now when we get a haircut, but we will be paying it. That is part of tax reform. I think that has been part of the tax reform that has been largely overlooked. I do not hear many Conservative Members talking about the new national sales tax that tax reform will impose on every Canadian citizen.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext: It is the second shoe.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
It is the second shoe, clubbed by the first one and then we will be booted by the second one.
How do we derive our revenues? Not many years ago, Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the amount of revenue which the federal Government collected from individuals and the amount collected from the corporate sector was about balanced, 50-50. Fifty per cent came from corporations and 50 per cent came from individuals. Over the years there has been some shifting as a result of successive Liberal and Conservative administrations.
If you look at those two sources of revenue now, 82 per cent comes from people and 18 per cent comes from corporations. That is the change. Who are the winners in this? The people of Canada have been taxed and taxed again. Under this Government, under every Budget it has imposed more taxes, more taxes and more taxes. There is a breaking limit, and for many Canadians we have reached that breaking limit now. People are saying that they are fed up and they will not pay any more income tax. They say they will find ways and means of avoiding the taxman or woman. So the underground economy begins to work. If you are a dentist, maybe you will fix some lawyer's teeth who will do some legal work for you and things will get done on a barter basis-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
-or on a cash basis with no receipts. Someone will come in and fix my plumbing for cash and there will be no record of that. Consequently, the price that work can be done
for is much less than normal. We all know that. Someone goes out into the woods and cuts a load of wood for fireplaces. He brings it into town and wants to be paid in cash, not because he wants to go out and buy something necessarily at that moment but because there will be no record of the transaction, and no tax has to be paid. The most recent estimates today would say that our underground economy in Canada is worth about S30 billion a year easily. Maybe it is significantly more than that. But that is what happens when people start losing confidence in the tax system. I suspect that for increasing numbers of Canadians that is where we are today.
In February and March of each year when you look into the book shops of Canada, what are the most sought after publications? What are the best sellers? They are books entitled, "How to Avoid Tax", "How to Defer Taxes," and "How to Shelter Taxes". People realize that our system today is unfair. It is discriminatory and unjust. Therefore, people say, "Well, if he does not pay any tax at all and is able to avoid all income tax, why not me?" That is a fact.
I am pleased to say the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had the courage to stand up the other day and say that there are hundreds and hundreds of wealthy people who pay nothing in income tax year after year, to say nothing of the 60,000 profitable corporations which pay no tax. When the small business person sees a large corporation like the Royal Bank of Canada paying not a penny in tax and a stock broker friend down the street paying no income tax year after year, people lose faith in the system. That is why we have called for at least a minimum tax on profitable corporations, not excessive, but a modest, minimum tax, so once again we can start building fairness and justice into our tax system. People will then not think of our tax as one designed for the greedy but one that is designed and composed for the needy.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I found the discourse very interesting in the sense that the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) said that Canadians are being taxed, taxed and taxed. I agree. But I find it somewhat ironic that it is the New Democratic Party and his Party's policy to increase social spending. We brought out a child care program for $6.3 billion, yet his Party said that it was not enough, that more money was needed. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in a debate that is important because it affects all Canadian taxpayers, including middle and low-income earners, men and women, those working in industry, and so forth.
The purpose of the tax reform, and everyone in Canada agreed that changes were necessary, was first of all to reduce income tax and other taxes paid by taxpayers; second, to ensure that any citizen, whatever his income, or any corporation that receives services in Canada should pay his fair share, and third, to simplify the process. If we look at the legislation before the House, it has failed to meet these three objectives.
First of all, Conservative Members and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) want us to believe, as when they told senior citizens they would not touch old age pensions, that personal income tax and other taxes will go down. That is not true. And I intend to prove it isn't because the Government has done a bit of manoeuvring, and if we compare 1984 to 1988, in 1988 it is going to cost taxpayers $26.7 billion more in income tax and other taxes they will have to fork over to this Tory Government, which means 62 per cent, while it will cost corporations only $2.6 billion or 28 per cent. Is that the promised balance between personal income tax and corporate tax? Why are taxpayers paying more income tax in 1988 than they did in 1984? Simply because the Government de-indexed the tax tables, which means de-indexation of personal exemptions and personal income tax.
For a family, it meant that family allowance and the child tax credit were de-indexed. It meant that the ceiling below which middle-income families were eligible for the child tax credit was lowered, and it meant eliminating the tax exemptions that could have been converted into a tax credit for families with children between the ages of 16 and 18, when children continue their education.
The Tory Government wanted more than just a bite out of our weekly pay cheque. Every week or every two weeks when people get their pay cheque, another tax credit has been cut, which means that for every $3 we now have only $2 left just because the Conservative Government has taken that dollar out of our pay cheque.
July 21, 1988

But the Government didn't stop there. It took a different approach, more hypocritical and less open, reflecting the style of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It used indirect taxes.
First we had three increases in sales tax on October 1, 1984, on January 1, 1986 and on April 1, 1986, from 9 per cent to 12 per cent. This means that every time consumers in Quebec and across Canada make a purchase, they are paying an additional Tory tax on all goods. This is a hidden tax. It doesn't show because the Government has already collected the tax from the manufacturer.
The Government didn't stop there. Gas was next, and what is more important than gas? Gas isn't just something you put in your tank to go on a holiday, to go for a drive. In Quebec, manufacturing is concentrated in the large urban centres, which means that essential products such as food, clothing and construction materials have to be shipped by truck. And trucks run on gas, which they need to deliver the goods to people in remote areas. And the same is true across Canada.
And the Tory Government, despite the fact that its gas expert promised to defend Canadian consumers in Ottawa, this Tory Government increased the price of gas by 23 cents a gallon. On September 3 1985, two cents a litre; on January 1, 1987, another cent; on February 19, 1987, another cent; and on April 1, 1988, one more cent. Mr. Speaker, all these increases in the tax on gas mean that when we open a bag of bread, drink a glass of milk or eat meat or fruit or vegetables, or when we buy curtains to decorate the house, the price increase doesn't go to the manufacturer or to the distributor. This is just another Tory ploy to increase the revenues of the Government. So much for the tax on gas.
But there is more. What about the tax on alcohol and tobacco, which has raised millions for the Government? But there are other examples, and I think the most shocking one, was the Prime Minister's failure to keep his promise to senior citizens. Last week, I had the honour and the pleasure of having lunch with Mrs. Solange Denis, the woman who said out loud on Parliament Hill what senior citizens were thinking, the woman who said: "Charlie Brown, you lied to us!". They remember. There is not one person in Canada, not one senior citizen who doesn't remember that the Prime Minister's word cannot be trusted. All senior citizens know perfectly well that the word of Tory Members cannot be trusted because they have already been cheated once, and it got to the point that senior citizens came to Parliament Hill and, as I said at the time, put down their playing cards and took up their placards to come and demonstrate to defend their rights.
However, the Government decided to increase the tax burden even more, reducing the purchasing power of Canadian taxpayers in the process. First of all, it put a sales tax that wasn't there before on soft drinks, snacks, manufactured construction materials and even on long-distance calls, Mr. Speaker.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
In the areas outside Montreal, the telephone is essential. If a child has an accident and his parents have to make a longdistance call to reach a doctor, there is a Conservative tax on each long distance call. I am talking about people in remote areas of Quebec, where Conservative Members were elected, Members who did not stand up to defend the population on such an essential service.
There is a tax on wallpaper, but what really tops everything is the tax on drugs. The Prime Minister and the Conservative Government discovered that they could make money on the backs of the sick. When it discovered that drugs were not taxed, this Government decided to go ahead and tax them- just imagine, no one is safe ... This medication isn't taken for the common cold, but by people suffering from cardiovascular diseases, respiratory illness, or diabetes.
Just as we did for the elderly, the Liberal team-smaller in number but a quality team nonetheless-had to band together with interest groups to force this inhuman and heartless Government to back down and withdraw the tax on drugs that are essential for survival. Unfortunately, the Government maintained its taxes on other drug products. This means that for the Conservative Government, a cold winter is a lucrative one-the more children with colds, the more children with the flu, the more money it makes, because it collects a 10 to 12 per cent tax on cold medications.
I have clearly demonstrated that there is no tax reduction for taxpayers and that their purchasing power is vastly diminished, because for each product they purchase they must pay the Conservative tax, either because of transport, or because of the sales tax on all the products that were not taxed previously and which the Conservative Government decided to tax.
I would now like to talk about the issue of fairness. In spite of the document we have before us today, there are still some 60 multinational corporations that will manage to benefit from advantages provided by the Federal Government and yet will not pay one cent of tax. And those businesses are not to be found in the Montreal-Sainte-Marie riding. These are not small family-run businesses where you have the father, the son and the wife all working hard-not the small car-repair shop or gas station-these are large multinational companies that are very close to the Prime Minister and whose representatives go to dinners at $5,000 and $10,000 a plate, and have managed to convince this Government to let them continue to abuse the system and continue to get off scot-free, without paying one cent of tax.
We saw figures again recently that showed that there are more than 5,000 people with incomes of $50,000 or more who do not pay tax, and others earning $100,000 or more who also pay no tax at all. Like middle and low-income earners, those people have the right to use health insurance and drug insurance programs; each one of us pays his share for those programs and we are forced to pay for the rich.

July 21, 1988

There you have proof that there is no fair treatment for everyone-corporations, the highest income earners, families and individuals with middle and low incomes-another failure. This reform has not achieved its objective.
As for simplifying the paper work, we expected, from what the Prime Minister gave us to understand, that people would find it much easier to fill out their tax returns. Mr. Speaker, here again, nothing has changed because the objective of simplifying paper work has not been met and tax forms have not been simplified, nor has the objective of eliminating tax loopholes for the rich; those loopholes still exist.
What should the Government have done? First of all, instead of granting a $500,000 exemption to the rich, while at the same time deindexing family allowances for low and middle-income families, rather than spending millions of dollars to bring in blue uniforms for the Armed Forces, it would have been preferable to continue helping our families.
But spending $16 or $17 billion for nuclear submarines is to my mind the greatest scandal of them all. Imagine that, Mr. Speaker-Canada decides that it could be under attack from two enemy countries! What countries are they? There are the Americans to the south and the Russians to the north. What weapons do those countries have? The Americans and the Russians do not just have two or three tanks. They do not have just one or two submarines, they have thousands. All of a sudden, our Canadian "Rambo", our new hero, decides to buy 16 submarines for a showdown with the Americans. He thinks that the American fleet will come here to Canada and want to get through. Then our "Rambo", our dear Brian, will jump into his submarine and say, "Hold on! If you shoot, I'll shoot!" Mr. Speaker, that is money wasted, poured down the drain!
We in the Liberal Party say no way will we have those 16 nuclear submarines. We won't do it. But what would we do with that money? With just one submarine, we can lower the pension age to 60 for all needy persons. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that your constituents in Duvernay, if asked, would rather lower the pension age to 60 than buy a single nuclear submarine. What would we do with the second submarine? We would put more money into day care and create more spaces. That takes care of two submarines and the money would help real people. What about the third and fourth nuclear submarines? What would we do with them? We would use the money to clean up the environment. We need it for the quality of life. That makes four submarines saved and many jobs for lots of people and better public services. What would we do with the fifth submarine? Our farmers in Quebec are penalized. Our farmers across the country need assistance, research and other such things.
So we would use the money from the fifth submarine for our farmers throughout Canada. There are still many submarines left for which the money could be spent in other ways. We could use the sixth and seventh submarines to establish a real family policy. Canada's number one problem is the low birth rate. What do Canadian families need? What do young couples need? Well, the sixth and seventh submarines could be
used to fully index family allowances, to increase the child tax credit for middle- and low-income families, to follow the example of a good Liberal Government in Quebec and give $3,000 for the first, second or third child to help couples.
Mr. Speaker, don't you think that the voters in your riding would prefer a family assistance and support policy to two nuclear submarines that will waste their time in the Arctic?
What would we do with the money from the eighth and ninth and additional submarines? First of all, we could use the money from two of them right away to reduce the deficit and stop the fussing inside the Government. But we also have our seniors, the elderly of today and tomorrow. What do our seniors most need, in addition to an income? What does every Member of Parliament hear from seniors? They do not want to go and live in an old age home. Seniors, even at 80 or 82, are in good physical condition and want to live at home, but they need help. Mr. Speaker, at 82, you cannot wash the ceiling and the walls. So we Liberals would use the money for the seventh submarine to set up a nice national program with the provincial Governments for home support, medical assistance, things people need, not submarines!
Young people, Mr. Speaker! We had programs that helped young people and we could take the money from the eighth submarine to help youth. What do our young people leaving high school, college or university need? They need work experience, because when they apply for a job, companies ask them if they have experience. Without it, they do not get work! So they go back to studying. Well, we could have a program like the one lawyers have; a lawyer works in the field for a year before taking the bar exam. We could take the money from a nuclear submarine to give every student a year of practical work experience with companies across Canada, whatever the occupation, be it engineer, architect, lawyer, notary, machinist, construction worker or docker, Mr. Speaker.
Another important aspect is the problem these days of people 30 to 55. Today, 40-year-olds who have a specific training see their working world upset by technological change. They see that they do not have an indexed pension plan; they do not even have a private pension plan. Well, we could take the money from two submarines to give these people with work experience phased-in retirement, Mr. Speaker.
How many 50-year-olds say to themselves, "My children are grown, my house is paid for, but I cannot stop working five days a week. But I could work three days a week and I would train a young person." That is what I was just talking about.
This is an overall policy for quality of life. That is what the Liberals will be fighting for in the next election campaign, a quality of life program. Quality of life begins at home. You want quality of life in your home, on your job, in your environment, around your house, in the air you breathe.
I conclude with that and I would hope that the Conservative Members will answer my questions. Why would the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) rather have the
July 21, 1988

Government waste $16 billion on nuclear submarines than use that money to lower the pension age to 60 for all seniors or for a home support program for seniors or to help young people or families? Member for Duvernay, unlike the time when he was head of the gas station owners in Quebec, allowed his Government to use gasoline as a way to get more tax from drivers or not tried to stop it, Mr. Speaker?
Mr. Speaker, I conclude and I would hope that some Conservative Members will wake up as the election approaches; otherwise, their time in Parliament will be short.

Mr. Speaker, I can appreciate why the Conservatives are not speaking on this Bill. There is nothing to defend. I can understand their unwillingness to participate and defend this Bill which is supposed to reform taxation. I can understand their shame and why they cringe and why they will not speak on this particular Bill.
It seems to me that any tax system must have three aspects to it. The tax system must be fair. The tax system must be progressive. The tax system must redistribute. Ordinary Canadians look at this so-called tax reform and they have to ask themselves certain questions. The first question has to be, is this tax system fair? There is a cynicism which exists with respect to what has happened since the Conservatives came to power in 1984, with all the hopes Canadians had that we would have effective tax reform. After all, that was one of their commitments during the election campaign. But what happened in the first three years in Government? The Conservatives taxed and taxed and taxed. They did exactly the sorts of things that the Liberals used to do.
In the year in which an election is expected, we get this much-touted so-called tax reform. Having taken out of the pockets of the average Canadian family over $1,000 over the last four years, the Conservatives decided to return it to them in their pay-packets. The Government says it is taking less from these taxpayers. This is all scheduled to happen, of course, on July 1, 1988, the eve of an election.
That is the first cynical aspect. Second, this Government has protected its options for an election next spring. Because of the so-called tax cuts in the spring of 1989, Canadians will get back a refund cheque. The amount that was collected in the first six months of 1988 will be calculated with a higher tax
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
deduction. That is cynicism. All of these so-called loopholes the Government says it has closed, none of that comes into effect until 1991. That is the other aspect of the cynicism. That is well beyond the next election. Canadians who are perhaps more cynical than myself would look at that and realize the opportunism of this Government when it comes to tax reform.
The Government is not really interested in reforming the tax system. It is a shell game. There is a pea under the shell and the Government moves the shells around. That is the old game that is played at fairs right across this country. That is a shame because I think it really destroys the whole political process. In fact, the political process is really the arena to make moral changes. It is a place at which Canadians should be able to look and see hope for a better system, for an improved system. But when we look at this tax reform package which is embodied in this Bill we find it sadly lacking. For example, the average Canadian will look at this tax reform package and discover that three out of four Canadian families earning over $100,000 a year, who have already benefited from past Budgets, will receive yet another tax cut of $4,363 per year.
The ordinary Canadian has to ask why, after this much-touted tax reform, the rich will again benefit. Average Canadians will wonder why a family earning under $15,000 a year will receive a cut of only $100 a year. Ordinary Canadians will ask why. Why this unfairness in the way this Government deals with the wealthy as opposed to the poor? Why is it that we have to take from the poor to give to the greedy? I suspect that is part and parcel of the Progressive Conservative ideology. It is part of that ideology that believes in acquisition. This is an age of acquisition. If one cannot go out and get it, there is something wrong. It is there for personal gain. As long as I can get my share, I do not care about any one else. That is the mentality that is reflected in this so-called tax reform.
Ordinary Canadians will remember the promise of a minimum tax. They will ask themselves why there is not a minimum tax on corporations. Why are the wealthiest corporations in this country treated with velvet gloves? Small businesses, in fact create most of the employment, 80 per cent of the jobs in this country. All of those who work very hard in their small enterprises, and individual Canadians who work very hard at their jobs, will ask why this Conservative Government treats the large corporations so generously and treats them with such severity in terms of taxation. That is a good question.
Why is it that after the so-called tax reform package, 60,000 very profitable corporations will still continue to pay not a penny of tax? That is a question Canadians will ask. After all, if those 60,000 very wealthy corporations do not pay their share to keep this country-a country which allows those corporations to make their handsome profits-someone else has to pay. That someone else will be the ordinary Canadian and the small enterprise. Canadians will ask why. Why does this Government do that?

July 21, 1988
Ordinary Canadians will take a look at the statistics which show that in 1984, when this Progressive Conservative Government came to power, the percentage of taxes collected from the corporate sector was 20.3 per cent of all revenues collected by the Government. The latest figures in 1987 show that it is down to 15.5 per cent. So corporate taxes have been reduced in terms of total contribution to the upkeep of this country, and the percentage of revenues the Government has taken from ordinary Canadians in income taxes and sales taxes has gone up considerably. So ordinary Canadians and small enterprises are paying more percentage-wise to support the country while the large corporations' percentage continues to decrease. The Government boasts that after these tax reform measures that figure will rise to 17.2 per cent by 1991. Big deal. That is still about three percentage points lower than they contributed when the Government came to power in 1984.
Ordinary Canadians will read that statistic and say: "Why? Is that fair? Is any of it fair? Is fairness reflected in this Bill regarding income tax reform?"
I see that it is time for lunch.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the lunch break I was commenting on the fact that there are three fundamental factors which affect every tax system. One of these factors is fairness, the other is the re-distributive nature of the system. The third factor is progressivity. I was talking about the fairness of the tax system. The Government in its proposal has scrapped the 10 rates and we are now moving to three rates. The top rate is somewhere in the vicinity of 44 per cent. Under the proposed so-called reforms in this legislation, all incomes above $55,000 will be taxed at a rate of 44 per cent. Any income above $55,000 will be taxed at a rate of 44 per cent. This means that families which earn just above $55,000 will face the same rate of taxation as a person who earns $1 million. The most striking aspect is that many Canadians with incomes of less than $30,000 will face a marginal tax rate of 39 per cent. Is that fair?
That is the question average Canadians are going to ask. Should a secretary at Bell Canada who earns $28,000 a year face a marginal tax rate of only 5 percentage points below the rate faced by the chairperson, Mr. de Grandpre, who earns some $900,000 a year? A secretary at Bell Canada will be paying the same rate of tax. Is this the Conservative view of fairness?
I also mentioned the fact that the tax system should be progressive. This Government, since it has come into power, has increased taxes. It certainly has increased the sales taxes
and it is even talking now about going to a national sales tax or what might be called a value-added tax or a business transfer tax. It is now going to proceed to one of the most regressive ways of raising taxes. Everything will now be taxed. If you go to see a lawyer to get your will drawn up, you will pay a tax. The Government is going to collect.
There are those who see a devious plot in all of this. In fact, when the free trade deal comes into effect, the Government is going to be giving up some $1 billion in revenue as a result of the tariffs it is going to forgo when products come across our border. That is $1 billion the Government cannot give up without getting it from somewhere else. So the Government has come up with this system of a business transfer tax to really recoup from the consumers of Canada what it will lose with respect to the free trade deal.
All of this talk about free trade being a bonanza for consumers is not correct. I hope Canadians are not thinking that somehow or other they will be able to get all these things a lot cheaper because there is no tariff duty on, for example, television sets coming in from the United States. I trust Canadians are not thinking that way because this Government is going to grab it all with this business transfer tax.
In the long run, the Government will be taking in spades more than it has given in tax reform. The most regressive form of taxation is sales taxes. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) goes to the store and buys bread, he pays the same price as a poor person. The tax does not respect wealth and it is not sensitive to poverty. It is a tax that is applied and everyone pays it. It does not recognize that some person might be on a fixed income of perhaps $15,000 or $16,000 a year. Just because they are on a fixed income does not mean the tax will be waived. It does not apply. The tax is regressive because it does not respect incomes. It is regressive and not progressive.
We New Democrats studied this whole question of taxation. It was one of our concerns. It was an issue for us in the 1984 election campaign, and it remains an issue for us today. The New Democratic Party caucus studied the tax system. We participated in the Finance Committee when it looked at tax reform, which has resulted in this Bill. Our members on the committee on behalf of the caucus tabled a minority report in which we made recommendations. I want to put those recommendations on the record.
First, we recommended that the structure of tax rates should be further examined and that a higher tax rate should be imposed on high-income Canadians. People such as Mr. de Grandpre should not be paying 44 per cent; they should be in a higher tax rate, those who have received so much from our country. They should be prepared to contribute much more to the upkeep of it.
July 21, 1988

Second, we have recommended that the personal income tax system should be indexed fully to inflation. We agree with moving from exemptions to tax credits. We agree that that is fair. But it is not going to be fair if we do not ensure that those tax credits are fully indexed to the cost of living. In fact, what the Government has tried to establish with tax credits is to redistribute wealth to those who need it. Unless provision is made for indexation to the cost of living, the value of the tax credit will be eaten up by inflation.
Third, we recommended that capital gains income, except for that of farmers and small business, be fully taxable, and the lifetime exemption be eliminated. The Government continues to allow capital gains up to $100,000 with a lifetime exemption.
That is a tax loophole that ordinary Canadians cannot take advantage of. They are not in the speculation business. They are in the living business. They have to live from day to day. They are not the ones who buy condominiums in Florida. They are not the ones who are in the flips of property in Toronto where the market is so heated. We are saying in this recommendation, as was said in the Carter Commission report on taxation, a dollar is a dollar is a dollar and it has to be taxed.
Fourth, we recommended that other personal tax measures which largely favour the wealthy such as the deduction for RRSP contributions for upper income earners, special treatment of dividend income and full deduction for interest costs in excess of investment income be further reduced. In 1984, 187 wealthy Canadians with incomes of more than $250,000 paid no income tax whatsoever. Many more paid tax at well below the average rates. By and large, this tax reform proposal of the Government does not change much. It still allows the wealthy to take advantage of loopholes in the tax system.
We believe there ought to be no sales tax on food whatsoever. We recommended that the reform of the federal sales tax should not involve taxation of food, and should reduce the reliance of the federal Government on indirect taxes.
We also recommended that special treatment for capital gains relative to other corporate profits should be eliminated. Tax measures which favour large profitable corporations such as the seven-year carry-forward and the two-year carry-back loss provisions and the deductibility of interest costs incurred in corporate takeovers should be reviewed.
Finally, we recommended that a corporate minimum tax be implemented. That was one of the promises we elicited from the Prime Minister during the 1984 campaign.
We say to the Government that these are the kinds of recommendations that would make tax reform tax fairness. That is what we are interested in, not this phoney approach to tax reform but rather tax fairness as outlined by the recommendations which this caucus put on the record in the Finance Committee as its minority report.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this important debate. I heard a few familiar words a little while ago from the Hon. Member who just spoke, although it was in different terms to what was said four years ago. I heard the ring: "Jobs, jobs, jobs". At one time it was said with disrespect, and now it is with respect. I have heard a lot of rhetoric from the NDP and previous speakers about loopholes. The Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap (Mr. Riis) was talking about dozens and dozens of loopholes, which apparently were studied in Tax Probe '86.
