Member would rise and say that there was absolutely no initiative there of any great economic consequence.
July 21, 1988

Besides the reforms initiated by this Bill, the record is quite clear as to what the Government has done in previous tax reform. A minimum tax has been initiated which was implemented to ensure that upper-income Canadians pay their fair share of tax. Tax shelters based on investments in yachts, recreational vehicles, and similar properties have been eliminated; income splitting through interest-free loans between family members has been halted; the so-called carve-out transactions in the oil and gas sector have been stopped; trusts are now unable to distribute investment income tax free; the use of partnerships and corporate takeovers to increase tax deductions has been eliminated; new at-risk rules for limited partnerships have been introduced; and corporations are being prevented from distributing profits as capital gains rather than dividends.
These are all initiatives that our Government has brought forward and these were so-called loopholes in the past. We have looked at various other initiatives that we have in place, and it is difficult to make major changes. Other than what we are bringing in now, I believe that what we are bringing in with this Bill certainly is fair and equitable. I am quite surprised that the opposition Members would argue against the initiatives of this Bill.
1 would like to point out particularly one of the key elements in the tax reform package, which is the conversion of personal exemptions and some deductions to tax credits. For more than 20 years, Canadians who have studied our tax system have increasingly recommended that tax credits should replace exemptions and deductions to make the system fairer.
The reason why tax credits are fairer is straightforward: An exemption or deduction is subtracted from income in determining taxable income. It is therefore of greater value to higher-income earners because it reduces income that would otherwise be taxed at a higher marginal tax rate. A tax credit, on the other hand, is subtracted from tax owed, and therefore provides the same reduction in tax to all taxpayers regardless of their income level.
Let me illustrate in dollar terms. A $1,000 exemption reduces the federal taxes of a taxpayer in the old 6 per cent tax bracket by $60. But for a taxpayer in the highest tax bracket, federal taxes are reduced by $340-almost six times as high. When the provincial portion is calculated, the higher income earner comes out even further ahead.
Under tax reform, this $1,000 exemption is converted to a tax credit equal to 17 per cent of income, which is $170 for a $1,000 amount of money. This amount will be the same for taxpayers in every tax bracket, whether low or high-income earners.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
The new tax credits will replace the personal exemption, the married exemption, the equivalent-to-married exemption, the dependants' exemptions, and the age exemption. Credits will also replace a number of deductions: The disability deduction, the pension income deduction, the medical expense deduction, the tuition fee and education deductions and the charitable donations deductions. The most commonly used credits have been set at levels that will make them worth more on tax savings for the majority of taxpayers than the old exemptions would have been worth.
Lower-income taxpayers, in particular, come out ahead. Indeed, the increased value of personal credits is the main reason why 850,000 lower-income Canadians will have their income tax reduced to zero.
Let us look at a few of the commonly used credits to see why they are better for 66 per cent of taxpayers in the 17 per cent tax bracket. The new basic personal credit directly reduces federal tax payable by $1,020. This year, the basic personal exemption would have been $4,270, reducing the federal tax by only $725; therefore, it is clear that most taxpayers come out further ahead.
The married or equivalent-to-married credit is set at $850. The old exemption would only have been worth $635. The age credit is $550, significantly higher than the $455 value of the exemption. The $65 credit for a dependent child is the same as the old exemption; however, for the third and subsequent child the credit is doubled.
Many deductions will also be converted into tax credits at 17 per cent of their present value. That is, taxpayers will be able to subtract from tax 17 per cent of the amount that they can now subtract from income. In effect, this simply means that the new credits are worth the same to those taxpayers in the 17 per cent bracket as the old exemptions. The conversion to tax credits directs more money to those in need and reduces the after-tax value of benefits going to higher-income Canadians.
Tax credits respond to the view, expressed to the Government by Canadians from one end of the country to the other, that the tax system should be fairer and give a better break to those most in need.
Tax credits also work to eliminate a number of inequities under the old system. A perfect example of this is the new married or equivalent credit. Dependent spouses will be able to earn $500 before their earnings begin to reduce the married credit. Above that amount, the credit will be reduced at the rate of 17 per cent of earnings. Under the old system, those earnings directly reduced the married exemption, which in turn increased the amount of income taxed at the highest tax rate of the higher-income spouse.

July 21, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
The credit system ensures that the initial earnings of a second income earner are effectively taxed only at the lowest rate in the system. This removes the disincentive under the old system for many spouses to enter or return to the workforce.
Tax reform also recognizes the importance of tax credits as an integral part of the Government's over-all social policy. The refundable child tax credit has become a vital measure aimed at assuring families of adequate income support for the care of children. The credit is being increased to $559 this year, up from $489 last year. It is now available for children in the year that they turn 18.
Combined with other tax reform measures and with the Government's child care proposals, the improved credit will significantly increase tax assistance for most families with children and make the system more progressive.
Similarly, the sales tax credit, which has increased under tax reform, serves a vital function in offsetting the effect of sales tax on those with medium or low incomes.
I might add that we have made clear that the sales tax credit will be enriched considerably and extended in the second stage of tax reform when a new, broad-based sales tax is introduced. The new two-tier credit for charitable giving will encourage charitable support by starting at 17 per cent for donations up to $250, and then rising to 29 per cent for donations above that level. The new credit means that tax assistance will now be based on the size of the donation, not the size of the donor's wallet.
No longer will we have an unfair system where the donation of a wealthy person is rewarded more than the donation of someone less well off.
Since provincial taxes, except in Quebec, are calculated as a percentage of federal tax, all the new credits will also have the effect of reducing provincial taxes in the provinces. For example, the charitable donations credit would actually be 25.5 per cent for the first $250 and 43.5 per cent for donations in excess of $250, in a province which levies a tax of 50 per cent of basic federal tax.
I am pleased that Quebec made a number of changes in its last Budget, to ensure that Quebecers can take advantage of some of the tax savings from federal tax reform.
With all of the advantages offered by tax credits in terms of fairness, social progress and flexible application, Canadians will agree that the time has indeed come to adopt them into the system as part of tax reform. I urge all Members of the House to support the Bill before us.

We have also seen this Government hide the thrust of its tax reform, using various measures as a smoke screen. A few months ago, for instance, we had some incredible tax increases, and now we have a Bill which admittedly introduces a number of tax cuts.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval gave an example which very aptly illustrates the situation. The example he gave was this: It's like a thief who steals an old lady's purse, opens it, removes $150, leaves $50 and gives the purse back to the old lady with the remark: I didn't rob you because I gave you back your purse. So I think that illustrates the Government's attitude in the Bill now before the House.
With previous measures the Government put an incredible tax burden on Canadians, and now it proposes a series of tax cuts.
More specifically, Mr. Speaker, over a four-year period there will be a reduction of $11.1 billion in personal income tax, an increase of $4.1 billion in corporate tax and finally, an increase of $5.4 billion in revenues raised by sales and excise tax. On the face of it, this may seem very attractive, but we must realize that considering the present situation, these proposals smack of electioneering, to my mind.
In recent weeks, we have seen what seemed to be a series of tax cuts, marginal though they may be. And there is also the fact that as a result of these measures, taxpayers will be entitled to a refund when they file their returns in April 1989. So all this is being planned to cover two eventualities. If an election is imminent, the Government could say: Look we cut taxes. If they decide not to call an election now or in the weeks to come, they can say next spring: Look at your tax refund. There's proof positive that we managed your tax money and this country both wisely and well.
July 21, 1988

1 think this shows how little respect this Government has for the Canadian people, if it thinks it can make Canadians forget what happened in the past four years. We saw this not long ago in a by-election, when the Conservatives promised incredible amounts of money in order to win votes.
The proposals before the House are altogether unacceptable for any number of reasons.
When we talk about tax reform, I think we should aim for improvement, but this improvement should be tangible and reflect a better distribution of the tax burden, away from those at the bottom of the financial scale to those who are better off.
The main criticisms are of course the fact that the new rate structure and tax brackets are not progressive enough and I think that the best way of illustrating that reality is through the following example: Take the case of a family with an income of $30,000; their effective tax rate would be 31 per cent, which is higher than the rate for a family earning $100,000. The family earning $100,000 would only be taxed at the rate of 29 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, consider also the following fact, which is just as indecent, just as unacceptable and just as unreasonable: Tax reform will allow 60,000 profitable businesses to continue to operate and do business in Canada, without paying one red cent of income tax.
According to the document we were given on tax reform, the number of profit-making companies that do not pay income tax has in fact been reduced from 110,000 to 60,000. Before reform, there were 110,000 compagnies that did not pay tax. With tax reform, there will be 60,000 businesses that turn a profit, that are lucrative, and that certainly contribute to the economy in their region, but they will pay no tax whatsoever. That's the truth, and even if it were the only factor, the only criticism levelled at the bill, I think we should vigorously oppose it.
Of these 60,000 businesses, 35,000 will not be subject to tax because of the deferral of loss provisions, and 25,000 will not pay tax because of their low profits and the various tax incentives still present in the system.
I don't think it is going too far to ask all businesses to put their shoulder to the wheel and take on their share of the tax burden in Canada. The fact that there are 60,000 businesses out there that are profitable, that are going concerns, and that pay no tax seems unacceptable and certainly very inappropriate to me.
Also, Mr. Speaker, with tax reform the Government has brought in a minimum tax. This Government said: It is totally unacceptable and unfair that some Canadian taxpayers manage to pay no tax whatsoever. So what is known as a minimum tax was brought in. And yet in 1986 there were 5,220 taxpayers with incomes of more than $50,000 who did not pay one red cent in income tax. Of these 5,220 taxpayers, 40 earned $250,000 or more, and the Government seems content to have brought about a simple improvement in the matter, since in 1985, there were 7,947 taxpayers with incomes

of more than $50,000 who also paid no tax. To my way of thinking that sort of thing is totally unacceptable in our tax system.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) claims that tax reform will improve the situation, and that 850,000 low-income individuals will be totally tax-exempt. We must understand, Mr. Speaker, that it is possible that 850,000 people will find that they no longer have to pay tax. But we should also understand that over the past four years, the Government has taxed these people unabashedly, and today turns around and says: We are fixing things so that you will no longer have to pay tax.
That dovetails quite neatly with the example my colleague the Member for Laval (Mr. Ricard) gave: We stole from you for quite a while. We'll give you back your purse with a penny in it. That's the proof that we didn't steal from you. That proves that we are generous. But I think that Canadian men and women will not forget what they paid out during the past four years and that they will be able to assess the situation quite accurately.
People have criticized the Bill on another account, and that complaint seems quite well-founded to me. For instance, if we compare the total amounts paid by the taxpayers in 1984 and in 1988, after the tax reform, we see that only households with incomes in excess of $117,000, I could tell you that although there are more than 80,000 people in my riding, those who earn $117,000 a year are few and far between. Well, people who do earn $117,000 a year will pay less tax in 1988 than they did in 1984. These households account for 1 per cent of the Canadian population. So we have families earning $117,000 in 1988 and they will end up paying less tax than they did in 1984. Need I say more? I think this is just one more very obvious and telling example showing that with all such measures this Government has done everything it could to make the rich even richer, to the detriment of poorer families.
Another fact, Mr. Speaker, is that the Government, ever mindful of the upcoming election, said that taxes would be reduced as of July 1. A good many Canadians will notice a marginal decrease, I agree, smaller tax deductions on their pay cheques. But, Mr. Speaker, let us bear in mind that they have been paying too much since January 1988, so much so that if an election is called for next spring these people will again notice that their tax refunds are bigger. As I pointed out earlier, the Government will then be able to say that it has reduced the tax load. That is nothing but hogwash! As it is, the deductions made since January 1988 amount to a grand total of $1 billion which the Conservative Government took right out of the pockets of Canadians, wrongfully because it had no right to collect that money which will have to be refunded when people file their tax returns next year, and of course the Government will not pay any interest on that money.

July 21, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I think that Canadians will indeed be able to see for themselves that the over-all impact of the four Conservative budgets and the tax reform will translate into a sharp drop in family benefits. The best example I can give you is that the tax load of individual Canadians has grown a lot heavier than the corporate tax load. Here are some interesting facts and figures: between 1984 and 1985, and 1988 and 1989, the tax burden has been shifting towards individual Canadians. Sure enough, the individual tax load, that is personal income tax plus sales and excise taxes, went up by $26.7 billion during these four years, a staggering increase of 62 per cent, compared with a corporate increase of $2.6 billion, or 28 per cent more. Between 1984 and 1987 therefore, the corporate tax load increased by 28 per cent while personal income taxes went up by 62 per cent.
In addition, for a number of years now the percentage of corporate taxes with respect to total budget revenues has been declining steadily. For example, 20-odd years ago, in 1961-62, corporate taxes accounted for 20.1 per cent of budget revenues. By 1984-85 the figure had dropped to only 13.2 per cent; in 1984-85, only 13.2 per cent of all revenues came from what we might call the corporate sector. This trend has been even more obvious since our Conservative friends took office: this year, barely 11.6 per cent of revenues come from corporations whereas, from 1984 to 1985, the take was 13.2 per cent, $11.6 billion this year. Of course, they could take credit, and quite wrongly, for the fact that a number of jobs were created and that subsequently taxes paid by those new employees fattened government tax revenues. I would like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that if this is so, then corporations also became more profitable, their profits increased and so their contribution to tax revenues should have gone up likewise.
I think, Mr. Speaker that those few comments show how this Government intends to make people forget those four years in which the administration indulged in an absolutely unbelievable tax grab on the backs of Canadians, and in order to more clearly illustrate, let me give specific figures in specific areas. In the area of indirect taxes, the sales tax was increased from 9 to 10 per cent on October 1st, 1984, not to forget of course that Conservatives came to power in September. On October 1st, 1984, they increased the sales tax from 9 to 10 per cent; as if this were not enough, on January 1st, 1986, they raised it from 10 to 11 per cent; and because this was still not enough, four months later, they increased the tax from 11 to 12 per cent. And on each occasion this brought in $1 billion here, $1 billion there, and another $1 billion. Who is paying the sales tax? I have no hesitation in recognizing that the rich, the less affluent and the poor pay it. But it must be understood that the sales tax is much harder, much more cruel to people near the poverty line. who use that type of product, people who eat that kind of food are mainly the general population, in other words people who do not have the ability to pay what this Government asked from them.

Air travellers-and this may not mean everyone but in the main I think we can say as a rule that they have greater ability to pay than the majority of the people who never boarded an airplane. However that tax only brought in $55 million. Fifty five million from a tax that at the outset was aimed at a much richer, much more affluent category of taxpayers out of which the Government could have gotten much more than $55 million.

There is no question that with the exception of employment, there is no issue of more vital importance to the people who live in my riding of Winnipeg North Centre than the issue of taxation. Therefore, I want to make quite clear where my Party and I stand on this issue and how 1 see the Government's approach to taxes.
What I hear from people is that they want and need justice in the tax system. They want tax justice rather than tax burdens. They want tax fairness rather than tax politics. I have concluded, and I am sure other ordinary Canadians have done the same, that the Government is playing politics with the tax system. When the Conservatives were elected they raised taxes in Budget after Budget after Budget. They raised taxes to the extent of $1,500 for the average family. Now that we are approaching a federal election, now that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is searching for the courage to call the election, now that he is peeking around the corners testing the winds to see whether or not it is all right to have an election, the Conservative Government has changed its direction on taxes and is going to give a few dollars to Canadians. After taking thousands of dollars out of the pockets of ordinary Canadians the Tories are going to give a few back.
The Tories hope Canadians will have very short memories. They hope the average Canadian will look at his or her pay cheque today and see that in comparison with the month before their take-home pay has gone up because federal taxes have dropped. The Government is hoping they will see that and say: "We have a good Government, we have a Government for the people". That is what the Government hopes. If Canadians have short-term memories and difficulty remembering as far as a few years back, in all likelihood they would come to that conclusion. However, that would be a very short-term perspective. I am sure it will not be the perspective of most Canadians because the average Canadian family knows that it has less disposable income today than it had four years ago and that it is worse off with regard to the tax burden than it was four years ago.
Those Canadians who voted for the Prime Minister, the Conservative Party, and change in 1984, voted for tax fairness. They were promised tax fairness and tax justice. They will remember that the same Government took the disposable income out of their pockets. It picked Canadians' pockets of the cash they had to buy the things they need for their families. This Government has raised taxes for the average Canadian family by $1,500 in a series of Budgets over the last four years.

July 21, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
Canadians have good memories and will know who to hold accountable. If the Government thinks Canadians will suddenly forget who took the money out of their pockets, just because they are being given a few coins back today, it is underestimating Canadians. Canadians will know that they are being toyed with and being underestimated. They will see through the cynical gestures of the Government and will measure the Government accordingly. They will know that the Government is playing politics with taxes in an attempt to win the next election rather than being committed to justice in economics and taxation for the ordinary family.
Canadians must remember to take the long look if they want just government and just taxes. I believe they will do that. I know that the families who live in my riding are fed up with constantly increasing taxes and having to carry the burden of the tax system while others are getting away scot-free. They know that others are being given gifts by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take a different approach to the issue. This Government is now trying to make Canadians forget the fact that it increased taxes, but who else would be responsible for such an increase? Is there an alternative for Canadians? The Liberal Member who spoke before me promised tax justice. Is the Liberal Party an alternative? Is it offering the possibility of tax justice?
While on the subject, I hope Canadians will remember the Liberals' actions when they were in power. It was a Liberal Government which introduced that system, reduced taxes for corporations and increased them for individuals.
It was a Liberal Government which increased taxes for ordinary families while reducing them for wealthy Canadians. It is not an alternative, Mr. Speaker, since the Liberal Party actually established a "Conservative" economic policy in tax matters. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, despite the wonderful promises made by Liberals when they were in the Opposition, once in power, they did not offer an alternative nor a true change of direction to ordinary people. They certainly make big promises, just like Brian Mulroney, the current Conservative Prime Minister, did! Both the Conservatives and the Liberals made big promises that they did not keep after being elected.
Mr. Speaker, people should remember that it was Mr. Turner, current Leader of the Liberal Party who, as Minister of Finance in a Liberal Government, introduced the policy of giving out tax exemptions to large corporations. Under that policy, corporations that make hundreds of millions of dollars in profit pay no taxes at all. That situation is the result of a policy put forward by a former Liberal Minister of Finance,
who is now Leader of the Opposition and the Liberal Party, which is now pretending to be in favor of tax justice-

I want to take a look at the issue of justice in the tax system from another perspective, from the perspective of who benefits from and who is hurt by the tax system. Clearly the rich and powerful and the largest corporations in the country do quite well by the tax regime which both Liberal and Conservative Governments have put in place.
We know that many individuals who earn over $100,000 a year pay not one cent of tax. We know that large and powerful corporations which make hundreds of millions of dollars in profit pay not one cent in tax. I am not talking about taxing corporations which are struggling to survive and to provide employment. I am talking about powerful, wealthy, lucrative, profit making corporations which are making hundreds of millions in profits and are paying no taxes.
We ask why, not only from the perspective of justice in the tax system but from the perspective of what we give up by giving up these revenues. What opportunities do we lose by giving up the revenues which could be collected from very wealthy Canadians who earn over $100,000 a year and large profit-making corporations? What could we be doing with those revenues? What could we be doing to introduce a greater measure of justice in Canadian society?
I would like people, including Members of this House and in particular members of the Government, to ask themselves that question. What could be done with the millions of dollars of revenue that is forgone when wealthy individuals and profitable corporations are allowed to get away with paying no taxes?
The Auditor General is an objective, independent officer of the House. He has identified some $40 billion of tax write-offs whose success in achieving their stated economic benefits are questionable. For example, it is questionable whether some of these write-offs achieved their objective of creating employment or enhancing research and development to provide a stronger economy.
While we ought to retain those tax incentives that achieve their objectives and produce the required results, tax incentives such as those the Auditor General pointed to, which do not achieve the public objective for which they were implemented and only benefit the interest of corporations and the wealthy who use them, ought to be closed. The revenues saved from closing those loopholes should be used to introduce a measure of economic and social justice in this country. I want Canadians to think about how they would use those revenues.
July 21, 1988

Many people in my riding complain about the heavy burden of taxation. While they had disposable income to spend as they wished some four or five years ago, all their money is used today on the necessities of life. Those people would like some tax relief.
1 spoke to a man in my riding who some four or five years ago was earning the minimum wage of $5 an hour and supporting a family. Now his wage is about $11 an hour, but he finds that his income has not gone up because of the taxes coming from his pocket. The Government has continued to increase the burden of tax so that he has received no benefit from the increase in wages.
1 have also talked to people in my riding who are known as yuppies. A married couple earning $40,000 a year each are discovering that rather than being able to afford the luxuries of life, their salaries are actually dropping as their taxes continue to rise.
At least some portion gained from the closure of these loopholes should be used for tax relief. The tax relief gained by requiring individuals earning over $100,000 a year and powerful corporations to pay tax would introduce a greater measure of economic justice and social justice in our society.
What about the homeless? While we have been drawing attention to the fact that the average Canadian in a city like Toronto and many other cities can hardly afford a house, we forget that there are many individuals, as well as families who have no house. These people deserve a roof over their head. Those children deserve a roof over their head. I suggest that some of the revenues gained from closing unproductive tax incentives should be used to provide that kind of accommodation.
Why not use those revenues to provide for the hungry in our society, or to give training to the functionally illiterate in our society?
We need an alternative under tax reform that will not be satisfied by the political games that the Conservatives are playing with the tax system. The Conservatives increased the burden of taxation when they were elected. Now they are giving back a few pennies as an election approaches. Canadians will not be satisfied with the promises of the Liberal Party that started us down that road.
Canadians must be made aware of the unjust tax system that increases the burden on ordinary families while it allows the rich and the powerful to go tax-free. We need a citizenry that will demand tax reform, with a Party that will take up the fight with them in order to bring about real justice in a tax system so that everyone will pay their fair share. Such an approach will mean a greater measure of economic and social justice so that no family will have to go without a roof over its head and no child in this society will have to live on the streets. I call for a serious approach to tax justice so that those who have pay and those who do not have receive the help they need.
Royal Assent
The Conservatives have only increased the tax burden on ordinary people. As we approach an election, they provide a little relief in the hope that people will forget who increased their taxes originally. The Liberal Party only gives big promises when in opposition but acts like Conservatives when in government.
Let us debate this legislation thoroughly so that Canadians will be aware of the nature of the tax system today. When they realize that large and powerful corporations earning millions of dollars in profit pay no taxes, they will demand change. When Canadians become aware that people earning over $100,000 a year pay no tax, they will demand justice.
Canadians know that they are paying more taxes today than they were four years ago when the Conservatives were first elected. They know they have less disposable income than they had four years ago. The election is the opportunity for them to hold the Government accountable for the fact that they have less to meet their needs than they had four years ago.
I call upon the people of Canada to wake this Government up and let it know that Canadians are interested in tax relief, not politics played with the tax system. Canadians are interested in tax fairness, not political stratagems. They are interested in fairness, not increased tax burdens. They want the Government to collect its just, fair revenues so that it can use them to bring about greater social justice in Canadian society, so that no one will have to go without a roof over his head or hungry, so that people can be trained to use their full capacity. We need tax justice and social justice in this country. We need a NDP Government.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) played on one of the simplest of emotions that could ever be portrayed before a citizen of any democratic country. He said essentially that citizens do not like paying taxes. That is quite understandable. No citizen likes to pay taxes if he or she thinks there is some legitimate way of not doing so.
The Member also played on the emotion that the hungry, the indigent, those who live in the streets, ought to have some significant assistance and help. I want to say to the Hon. Member that no Member of Parliament, no matter to what political Party they aspire or work for, believe that these grossly wrong social injustices are appropriate in any society.
Having said that, let me also remind the Hon. Member that when our Government came to office in 1984, and it is still a fact today, one out of every three tax dollars did nothing other than service the accumulative debt of this country.
The Hon. Member cannot have it both ways. Let us pretend for the moment that there was no debt. In that case, Canadians could pay one-third less taxes or, alternatively, pay for one-third more services. I would be greatly interested to know
if the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre believes it is appropriate that one out of every three dollars that every citizen pays in taxes to the Government of Canada should be used for nothing other than to pay interest on debt? Is that good value for Canadians? Is that why we should pay our taxes? If the answer to that is no, if the Member says, "no, that is not good value", then how is he going to bring that debt down?
Canadians should be told that it is a burden placed there by a Government past because of its wild spending habits in the years from 1972 to 1984, and that it was supported by the NDP. The NDP endorsed the Government's National Energy Program. It was those kinds of expenditures that drove the debt, year after year, higher and higher. I would like to hear the Hon. Member's response.

He knows that the coming into office of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is what brought about the trend, to where almost 1.5 million more Canadians are employed. They are now in a position to pay taxes, to help spread the burden, and to bring down the debt.
I ask the Hon. Member: Is a major significant debt good for Canada? If the answer to that is no, then what other option is there to pay that debt other than what we have already succeeded in doing, that is, increasing employment in this country and making sure that all Canadians together shoulder the burden to get rid of the albatross that takes one out of three of our tax dollars?

The first Government was the Government of Tommy Douglas. When Tommy Douglas was elected during the Great Depression, the Province of Saskatchewan was deeply in debt. Tommy Douglas was a man, a leader who was concerned about social economic justice. He managed over the years to bring down that debt. At the same time, he increased social services and social justice in the Province of Saskatchewan.
To pose the false dichotomy of bringing down debt and increasing social justice is simply a rhetorical trick the Member seeks to play. I want to point to the behaviour of his own Government. How can this Member stand and point the finger at the New Democratic Party, saying that we are responsible for the debt when his Party has just gone through the process of buying a by-election? It was a "buy-election" in Lac-Saint-Jean. It cost hundreds of millions of dollars. That Party is now in the process of attempting to apply that very same strategy, that "buy-election" strategy, to the whole of Canada. That Party is seeking to buy the Canadian voters with their own money.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one is interrupted by Her Majesty, one always yields graciously.
Before the knock on the door I was indicating that in the early part of 1987 Canada Post had removed a number of street mailboxes from my constituency of Burnaby. I intervened on behalf of my constituents and was successful in having a number of them restored. This affected both residents in the area as well as a number of businesses, including Transport Equipment Control Systems whose President, Mr. Bob Nakashima, sent a note along saying that he appreciated very much the work that 1 had done on his behalf as his Member of Parliament to restore postal service in his area.
Some might ask why is it necessary to pursue this question of postal service at this time some 15 or 16 months later. Under the Conservative Government the quality of postal services has declined and the cost has gone up substantially. This is still a very timely and an important question.
New Democrats have taken a clear stand on the Post Office, particularly the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) and the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar). The New Democratic Party strongly believes that door-to-door delivery should be extended to all suburban residents and that all urban residents should be treated equally. We have opposed the corporate plan of Canada Post since it was approved by the Conservative Cabinet and tabled in the House last fall.
Let us look at some of the elements of this corporate plan which will have a disastrous effect on the quality of postal service in Canada. It calls for the elimination of 8,700 jobs and the closure of some 5,200 rural post offices across Canada. There will be an increased centralization of mail sorting, which will lead to even more delays in mail delivery. There will be the privatization of counter services to inadequate retail outlets and the replacement of door-to-door mail delivery with so-called supermailboxes.
In other words, effectively what Canada Post is doing is dismantling the service over a period of some 10 years. As New Democrats we believe in this public service. We believe that the Post Office is an important and a vital service. We believe that we should allow the Post Office to expand and get into areas in which it can make money, gain revenue, and
Canada Post Corporation
cross-subsidize some of its less profitable operations. That has been done by the Post Office in Great Britain and the Post Office in Australia very successfully. I suggest that we look at the same kind of thing here in Canada.
Today some 54 per cent of Canadians receive door-to-door service. That percentage will drop dramatically over the next 10 years under Tory cuts in postal service. This is an issue of basic fairness, for those who live in communities across this land are entitled to that door-to-door delivery and should not be treated as second-class citizens because they happen to move into a suburban area which does not have the service.
I received a letter from a constituent, a Mr. Geoffrey Thomas who said:
We are generally very satisfied with the postal service however we just moved into our first home (townhouse) to find that our mail is not delivered to our door. We must walk every day to a commercial post box to pick up our mail. This is unreasonable since homeowners in Burnaby have door-to-door delivery. I would appreciate an explanation for this situation.
This constituent is certainly entitled to that explanation. We know that the failure to provide door-to-door postal service hits particularly hard the disabled and our senior citizens. We know as well that letter carriers play an important role in the course of their daily delivery. They are not just delivering mail but in many cases they perform an important social function, particularly with elderly people. They check on them and make sure they are okay. For some elderly people this is virtually their only contact with the outside community. Now they are being told to walk several hundred yards to pick up their mail at some sort of a big supermailbox. That is unfair.
What is the rationale for this cut in service? It is set out in a letter to me as follows:
Due to the rapid rise in housing starts, Canada Post has been faced with the fact that the cost of providing door-to-door delivery to all new homes is prohibitive, without massive increases in postal rates or greater dependency on taxpayers' dollars.
What absolute nonsense that is. This same Government which refuses to extend door-to-door delivery across this land is prepared to spend in excess of $8 billion on nuclear submarines. What kind of a twisted priority is that? To refuse to provide door-to-door service and to cut back on over 5,000 rural post offices at the same time as it is squandering taxpayers' money on nuclear submarines is absolute madness.
This applies not only to residential communities but also to industrial parks, for example. A Mr. Keith Beedie, one of my constituents, is a business person in Burnaby. He noted that he and a number of his business colleagues have put together an industrial park in Port Coquitlam called the Meridian Industrial Park. They wanted to get postal service at each of those businesses. What were they told by Canada Post? They were told to forget it, that Canada Post was not prepared to give them the service that the businesses across the street have had for decades. We as New Democrats do not accept that kind of abdication of responsibility.

July 21, 1988
Canada Post Corporation
Further, I note that in the lower mainland of British Columbia, a new franchise has been opened in a 7-Eleven store in Lynn Valley, North Vancouver. This has been criticized severely by the postal workers involved because the work that was formerly done by its members will be done by non-union employees at low wages and under conditions that are quite unsatisfactory. This attempt to franchise operations in 7-Eleven stores not only results in far lower wages and poorer working conditions but results in poor postal service, and 1 will come to that in a moment.
I mentioned rural post offices, and I want to take this opportunity to place on the record the concern of Canadians in rural communities across the land about the shutting down of rural post offices. I recently spoke out in Chilliwack, British Columbia, where many residents expressed their concern about the fact that the sub post office at Cultus Lake, British Columbia, which had been there for many years, had burned down recently. Canada Post is saying that it will not replace that sub post office, that it will open up a post office in some 7-Eleven store or another store that is open 24 hours a day. Hundreds and hundreds of the residents of that community have signed a petition asking for the service to which they are entitled.
I would note as well that in the case of rural post offices, it is women who are disproportionately hit because I believe over 80 per cent of rural postmasters are women. This is the only source of income for many of these women, and they are being told that their jobs are gone. They will be replaced by people making the minimum wage at local stores. That is Tory economics, and we reject harsh and unfair Tory economics.
Some time ago, I held a public forum in my constituency on postal service, and I also sent out a questionnaire about postal service to my constituents. I think the results are very interesting and 1 would like to share them with Members of the House. Some 71 per cent of those who responded to my questionnaire were dissatisfied with postal service. They said that the quality of postal service had gone down. In excess of 80 per cent had had mail either lost of damaged. Over 85 per cent strongly believed that there should be universal door-to-door delivery.
The main complaints cited by my constituents of Burnaby would, I am sure, be echoed by constituents across Canada, whether in rural communities or in urban communities. The largest complaint by far was the complaint about delayed mail.
I heard about this issue time and time again. We know that the advent of these private sub post offices will mean even more delays.
Damaged and lost mail was another concern as was the increasing amount of junk mail. People are getting fed up with the amount of junk mail they are receiving. As well, they were concerned about long waits and high postal rates while service is going down. Finally, they are seriously concerned about the so-called supermailboxes. They point out, for example, that among discarded junk mail has been found valuable mail like
personal cheques. They have been interspersed in the junk mail and have been lost. These are the kinds of concerns that have been raised.
We as New Democrats have concrete proposals to improve the quality of postal service. We are opposed to the recent cuts in service. We support universal door-to-door delivery. We oppose the closing of postal services.
I want to pay tribute to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, who has led the battle for New Democrats on this question and has done an outstanding job in bringing to the attention of Canadians the concerns particularly of rural Canadians but also of urban Canadians about the decline in postal service.
Finally, we believe in the expansion of postal services in Canada. We believe in selling more packaging materials, introducing electronic mail, and allowing banking services in post offices the way they do in other jurisdictions and the way we did in the past. Postal workers themselves have a number of concrete suggestions for improving the quality of service, including the addition of revenue-generating services, consumers' post, financial services, and bill payments. They suggest that Canada Post should get into package distribution and electronic bulk mail services. They note that the British Post Office has expanded its services in this area and has become profitable and even more efficient. The British Post Office has service six days a week, twice a day, yet it makes a profit. Why can we not learn some lessons from that postal system, pioneered by the Labour Government of Britain, 1 might add?
The postal workers also suggest that a major initiative should be taken to reduce workplace injuries and work-related illnesses by improving working conditions. In too many cases, the working conditions of postal workers are primitive. One of the worst safety records in Canada is with Canada Post. Canada Post spends in excess of $20 million annually as a result of workplace injuries. Finally, the workers note that adequate staffing is absolutely essential in order to be able to perform services efficiently.
In drawing to the attention of Hon. Members these concerns with respect to postal service, not just in my own constituency but across Canada, I would like to mention some specific concerns that were raised by the postal workers in a recent submission to the Burnaby Municipal Council, a submission made just last month. The concerns that were raised by postal workers in Burnaby are concerns that have been raised by postal workers across Canada, in Hamilton, in Winnipeg, in Quebec-all over Canada.
The postal workers noted that the new plan involving sub post offices and franchises involves a carded parcel system which will mean delays in picking up registered mail at post offices. Before May of 1987, if a person was not at home when a registered letter or parcel was delivered, he or she would get a card telling him or her to go to the nearest post office to pick
July 21, 1988

up the mail or the parcel. Now people get cards telling them to go to the nearest pharmacy, drugstore, or retail postal outlet. For the residents of Burnaby and other places, that means a delay in mail service. It means at least two days' further delay because that registered mail or parcel has to be taken back to the post office, then to the franchise operation. That means delay, and Canadians are fed up with delays in the postal system. This means even further delay in receiving important registered mail.
As well, in too many cases the cards that are left in the mailboxes do not even have telephone numbers on them that would allow people to contact the sub post offices in question to find out if the parcels are big or small. That makes a difference for senior citizens. They have to know if they will be able to carry the parcels, and they cannot find out if there is no telephone number on the card.
As well, the operators of these little sub post offices which are not run by Canada Post, sub post offices in drugstores, grocery stores and so on, are offering postal services as a sideline. They are more concerned with selling groceries, diapers, and the like than they are with first-class postal services.
There are concerns about the security of mail in these places. Other concerns deal with the lack of training and lack of familiarity with postal products and regulations. There is a high staff turnover because in many cases these are minimum wage jobs, language difficulties, and real problems with difficulties in handling the volume of parcels and mail at Christmas. Sometimes staff are simply spread too thin to give decent service.
The bottom line is that staff in these little grocery stores and so on are not trained to handle postal services. They are trained, if at all, to do the kind of routine work involved in a grocery store, not the important work of postal workers. I would note that the permanent and relief clerks at the South Burnaby postal station have a total of something like 17 years and 4 months of experience in serving Burnaby residents. The same is true of the clerks in the North Burnaby postal station.
Instead of opening up even more of these sub post offices, we should be expanding postal service by, for example, opening a New Directions outlet under the operation of Canada Post in the Brentwood Mall in Burnaby. This would be an important and viable expansion of service. If we continue the way we are going, both the South Burnaby and the North Burnaby postal stations will be shut down in the future, and that is something that the residents of Burnaby are not prepared to accept.
There are other dangers as well. 1 mentioned already the question of supermailboxes and the importance of providing revenue-generating services within the system. We believe that Canada Post should be putting service before profit, but we
Canada Post Corporation
also believe that it can achieve both those goals by expanding the range of services it offers.
In short, we say no to the closure of rural post offices. We say no to cut-backs in the quality of service. We say yes to universal, door-to-door service across this land. We say yes to a quality post office in Canada. We reject the attack by the Conservative Government on postal service in Canada.

Let us come to the nuclear submarines because that demonstrates something about the NDP as well. They talked about the $8 billion cost of nuclear submarines. They conveniently forgot to say that it was spread over 20 years. That is a very small price to pay to be a partner in NATO, a group of countries that have come together to ensure the freedom of Canadians, among others. Given that, we will play our part to ensure that this group of nations will always remain free. The Hon. Member talked about cuts in postal services. He then went on to refer to "the Tory cuts in postal services". He calls it government cuts. We on this side cut the postal service. Yet the NDP, along with the Liberals and ourselves, supported the idea that Canada Post be set up as a crown corporation.
What does that inconsistent political Party really believe? They voted for the Crown corporation. Are they really saying now that they want a Crown corporation but they want the Government to manage it? Surely, members of the NDP have to sit at one end of the teeter-totter or the other. They cannot scream that the teeter-totter is too high when it is up, or complain they are having no fun when it is down. The fact is they voted for the Crown corporation, they got the Crown corporation, and they cannot stand in this House and tell the Government to run it.
The Hon. Member then talked about the elderly. He had them jogging halfway across Burnaby to get their mail. He said that they had to walk several hundred yards. That is a good point. That is why his point of a walk of several hundred yards is wildly wrong. That is not what the plan says. It is to be within walking distance for seniors, yet he misses the point.
The Hon. Member opposes 24-hour post offices. He does not want Mac's Milk, 7-Eleven, and all the rest of these outlets running extended hours post offices, yet he turns around and champions women. He says that the NDP love the women out there and that the majority of workers at the post office are women. If there are less people working in the post office, he says that somehow puts women down. That is an interesting and strange piece of logic, but let me give him some bits of information that he might find useful. Whether we like it or not, only one woman out of six is like the traditional family where the man works and the female is at home with the children.

I shouldn't say working. I apologize for that instantly. I do not mean to imply that. I mean "employed". Anyone who has ever been in the home or ever been a mother knows what absolute full-time work is. I meant to use the word "employed".
The fact of the matter is that today most families have both partners working out in the community. Under the system advocated by the Hon. Member for Burnaby, by the time they come home the post office has been closed for an hour. Under the old system of the old dinosaur Party the post office is usually located downtown in the big building with the tower and the clock, with no parking for blocks around. It is never
open except when you are at your employment, and often it is closed over the noon hour.
That is what the Hon. Member for Burnaby proposes for the modern society rather than the shopping centres with parking areas and extended hours, that is, the kind of situation which is appropriate today.
The Hon. Member for Burnaby talked about junk mail. I have only received one piece of junk mail in my life. It was a request for money from the New Democratic Party. I took one look at it and said that I was going to write to someone because they were sending me junk mail. If there were in fact a category of mail called "junk mail", no one would send it. I agree that there are receivers of mail who sometimes do not like what they are getting, who wish they did not get this flyer or that brochure. When I return from my home in western Canada I am always amazed at how many new pizza companies have opened up in my area. Their flyers are always under my door, and I already eat too much pizza as it is.
However, the people who send the mail and the flyers do not think they are junk. If it were truly junk to the senders they would soon quit sending it. They do not send this mail only to watch their bank account go down. It is only junk to some of the recipients. People send that mail with a purpose in mind. For the Hon. Member to make that submission is, in fact, to deny the entrepreneurship of many people in the business community.
This inconsistent Member, who is only consistent in his inconsistencies, then said that the 7-Eleven and Mac's Milk stores are awful places, that they are terrible places to work and are insecure, et cetera. Later on he said that Canada Post has one of the worst safety records in the Canadian enterprise. This fellow would have everyone walk to the sender to pick up their mail. He cannot have it all these different ways. The argument must be better developed than that.
In all fairness to the Hon. Member, post office concerns have always touched the hearts of everyone in urban and rural Canada. It is important for him to remember that the Canada Post Corporation will show a profit next year. It has already been demonstrated that there is a speed up in the turnaround of mail. The operation of the Post Office is becoming more efficient. There will be more and more postal outlets as a result of the new Canada Post Corporation plan. I thank the Hon. Member for bringing this issue to the floor of the House of Commons, because I think people will now recognize that we are in fact on the right track.

Mr. Speaker, I represent a riding in the heart of Montreal, the beautiful riding of Hochelaga-Maisonneuve. For the benefit of those who aren't familiar with the neighbourhood, this is next door to the Olympic Stadium. A few years ago, a decision was made to build housing units on what used to be the Angus yards. So far, there are about 5,000 new residents. There are six or seven units for the elderly, and this week, I met one of the directors of the well-known Lucie-Bruneau Institute which is involved in integrating the disabled in housing co-ops, in housing units.
Today, I think we have to give some serious thought to the fact that beyond political Parties and ideologies, there are certain situations that must be dealt with. The director of the institute told me that in my riding, on the Angus property alone, there are 300 disabled persons in wheel chairs. How can you expect these people to pick up their mail, even if they have the best possible superboxes in the world? It was decided the boxes would be located on the street corner, but we are talking about disabled persons who cannot deal with this. We have elderly individuals who are 82, 87 and 89 years old. They have trouble walking. They are ill, they are tired, they are exhausted. They couldn't pick up their mail even if those boxes were made out of solid gold!
I wrote to the President of the Canada Post Corporation. I received an acknowledgement, informing me that he would look at the situation, but he never sent a reply. The injustice of the situation is appalling. These are Canadian taxpayers just like everybody else. They have the same rights and privileges and are entitled to the same services as the guy on the other side of the street who is in perfect health and gets his mail delivered. That is the honest truth.
I understand the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson). He has problems in his riding, and in our Party, we have people who have problems with those damned boxes. They are no good. I am against the whole principle, and I want to ask my Government and my Minister and to the President of the Canada Post Corporation as well, a corporation that is a Crown corporation, and I know it means we can't always get these people to do what we want them to do, but I ask him to give this his special attention. In the heart of Montreal, right in downtown Montreal, the mail is being delivered on one side of the street and not on the other. It doesn't make sense. This is unacceptable, and 1 think the Hon. Member for Burnaby is to be commended for presenting this motion, and I support it one-hundred per cent.

Mr. Speaker, when I was speaking on the main motion before we proceeded to Private Members' hour, I was making a point about the hypocrisy of the members of the New Democratic Party who express their opposition toward tax breaks except when it deals with an issue like flow-through shares. We all recall the flip-flop of the finance critic and House Leader for the NDP. One minute his Party was against flow-through shares and the next minute, when they realized that the Liberal Government's introduction of flow-through shares had resulted in the creation of thousands of jobs, they changed their mind.
Canada has the most competitive steel industry in the world. The heart and soul of that industry happens to be in my riding, where I represent Local 1005 of the United Steelworkers of America, as well as Dofasco which recently was involved in a bid to acquire Algoma, which would make it potentially the No. 1 steel producer in Canada.

July 21, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
Stelco, Dofasco and Algoma are very competitive because Liberal governments, through tax policies that allowed accelerated write-offs, encouraged companies to upgrade their steel-making capacity so that they could compete on a worldwide scale. While we may hear the NDP say that this type of tax incentive is a corporate rip-off, and would deny such a tax incentive, when it comes to actually eliminating an accelerated write-off to a company like Stelco or Dofasco, or eliminating the flow-through shares, reality hits the NDP hard. Reality dictates that there are certain tax incentives that can be introduced by governments to help business, particularly small business in this country, remain competitive with other countries.
Unfortunately, the NDP would like to play both ends through the middle. They criticized our past record for tax incentives. They also criticized the Liberal Party for believing that when there is an opportunity to assist Canadians, one should try to assist those at the lower end of the income scale.
I am not sure what the NDP would do, but there is a distinct difference in the approach taken by the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party in relation to tax policy.
One example is the area of child care, which has had much discussion in the last number of months. The Government's position with respect to child care is that there is only a certain amount of money that can be allotted to assist families facing this desperate need. If one follows the Conservative philosophy, why would the Government introduce a policy on child care strictly from the taxation point of view, which permits child deductions as opposed to child credits? The Government has potentially doubled the tax deduction available for parents. For a high income earning Canadian like myself, with the salary I receive as a Member of Parliament, the tax deduction will mean two or three times more money in my pocket than that for a steelworker or cleaning lady claiming the same deduction.
A cleaning lady in my riding works for a minimum wage of $4.50 an hour. She will not benefit from the child deduction in the same way as I will benefit.
If the Liberal Party had been in power for the introduction of a child care package, we would have told Canadians that we recognize that each family has a responsibility to be involved in the raising of their children, including financial involvement when it comes to child rearing and organizing for child care. At the same time, there are many Canadians in the middle class, particularly in the $25,000 to $30,000 a year range, who are being attacked from all sides. According to the Government's policy, rather than introducing a credit that will give the cleaning lady a better financial return than a Member of Parliament, it is giving more tax deductions to assist the higher-income individual to a much greater degree than a lower-income individual.
Even if we accept the amount of money that the Government is considering, we believe that the portion being set aside for family deductions should have been directed toward tax credits so that a mother working outside the home and earning perhaps $15,000 to $20,000 a year will be able to get a larger
return on her income tax than the mother who was earning $50,000 or $60,000 a year.
That would be sane tax policy. It is a fair tax policy which recognizes that the role of Government is to redistribute from those who have to those who have not. It would give those women in the middle class the opportunity to go out and participate in the paid workforce if they so choose. We should have the opportunity to be able to remain at home and look after our children if we have the tax base that gives us that support. Unfortunately, the Government's policy has resulted in an erosion of support for the family. The family allowance was deindexed. This suggests to me that the Government is not prepared to give the same kind of support to people with children.
The principle is simple. Someone who earns $40,000 a year and supports a spouse and children should be able to pay less tax than a single person earning $40,000 a year who can spend their disposable income on one person. Such a policy indicates support for families, rather than cutting back on family allowances. This so-called tax reform has the largest tax increases in the history of this country. According to the Government's own figures, the only people who will be able to take advantage of tax reform are those earning over $117,000 a year. That is not tax reform, that is tax robbery. It is tax robbery of the middle class in particular by a Government that realizes its mandate was not to serve the ordinary man and woman.
This mandate was to serve the big moneyed operators who are able to take advantage of the half million dollar capital gains write-off. That was one of the first actions of this Government. Ordinary Canadian men and women are taking it at the gas pumps. There has been a total increase of 27 cents a gallon since this Government came into power. They are taking it in indirect taxes. The average family is now paying over $1,000 extra in taxes. The people who are being helped out are the high-income earners like the person who can take advantage of the capital gains exemption and the person who is earning over $117,000 a year.
We do not believe that is tax reform. We think this document is a fraud. We think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government are about as honest in this particular venture as they were when they told senior citizens that their pensions would never be touched. We hope the Prime Minister and the Government will have the courage to call an election so that the people can decide for themselves whether or not they want to face these exorbitant tax increases.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to support the amendment moved by the Liberals on the tax legislation, but I think you realize, Mr. Speaker, that I probably would not accept all the words of the previous speaker from the Liberal Party, especially those words which were critical of the New Democratic Party.
It is obvious to many in this House and across this land that there is a need for real tax reform. The sense of unfairness Canadians have with respect to our tax system is not just a feeling held by a small group of Canadians, it is a feeling held by many, many Canadians. During the last federal election campaign, there was a debate on a minimum personal tax. It was our Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broad-bent), who raised that during the Leaders' debate. He pointed out that many of the richest Canadians were not paying one cent of income tax because we had created so many categories they could use for exemptions and so many investment loopholes they could use. They were not paying one cent in taxes. As a result of the debate that took place during the last election campaign, we finally had a minimum tax put in place for individuals. We have some problem with the tax that was put in place because we believe there are still some loopholes and ways that some Canadians can avoid paying their fair share of taxes.
One of the things that did not happen is we did not make the same provision for corporations. So we are now in a situation where corporations in this country which are making money- and we are talking about a significant amount of money-are not paying any taxes whatsoever. We do not believe that is fair. We know that other nations have looked at that situation and have said it is not fair. If we believe that individuals should pay their fair share, that those in the higher income brackets should pay their fair share, that there should be a minimum tax to guarantee they pay at least something, then the same thing should apply to corporations. That is something that many European countries and others have accepted as only natural. We believe that that is something with which this tax reform legislation should be dealing. The subamendment I will be putting forward in a few moments will deal with that aspect.
We believe that it is important that people pay their fair share. We also believe that corporations should pay their fair share. There are a number of problems with our tax system. One of the problems pointed out in my riding is the whole northern tax benefit. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that until the end of April 1988 some communities in the North were
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
allowed to deduct a northern tax benefit which saved many families about $2,000 to $3,000 a year in taxes. However, other communities, such as the community of Thompson and Wabowden in my riding, communities in northern Ontario and communities right across this land, north of the 56th parallel, were not deemed to be northern communities. Because of an outburst of protest from these people that they are indeed northerners, the Government acted on an interim basis and the people of Thompson, which is a community of 15,000, and the community of Wabowden in my riding, which is a community of 1,000 people, are to be temporary northerners. For the next two years they will be treated as northerners in the tax system until the Government straightens out its act. There was a study of costs in northern communities, and there might be some new legislation brought forward at that time.
I bring this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, as an example because I think it points out the problems we have with our tax system. Over a period of time the Government has made decisions but has had to back down. It has ordered studies and has changed its tax system rather than come to grips with all the problems we have with our tax system.
In many ways, I think people who are filling in their tax forms every February, March or April must feel they are playing a shell game. They do not know what the rules are, what they should have done a year before when they received their pay cheques. They really do not know what they should do to look after themselves and their families in terms of paying their fair share of taxes, but not paying more taxes than their neighbours. In an ironic situation, a bank teller earning a very small salary finds out he is paying more in taxes as a bank teller than the bank itself is paying. How does he feel? He cannot belong to a union because every time a teller or someone else tries to form a union, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce breaks that union by transferring people out. These people receive low salaries and then the tax system makes them pay a certain amount of taxes, but their employer has not paid a cent in income taxes for the last number of years. How do they feel about the fairness of the situation then?
In some ways the system the Government has presented is a step in the right direction. We are calling for a much fairer program. I know our finance critic, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) has spoken before, and I am sure he will speak again this evening, to explain why the system is not fair and what we could be doing to improve the tax system to ensure fairness for the average Canadian family. Wealthy families will receive an average of $4,365 a year in tax cuts, 60,000 profitable corporations will continue to get away without paying any tax at all and the average Canadian family is left paying $1,000 a year more in income and other taxes than they did in 1984.

July 21, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
What has happened? We have tax reform. Many of the corporations, not all of them, are not paying any tax. Wealthy families are going to receive a very substantial tax cut. Elowever, when we take a look at the entire situation, we find that most Canadians will be paying more in taxes after this tax reform measure than they did in 1984 when the Conservative Government was elected.
I only have 10 minutes to try to cover the whole taxation field, and that certainly is impossible. However, in the few minutes I have left there are two things I want to point out. First, I want to put forward an amendment, as I indicated earlier, and second, I want to say that we have not dealt with the whole question of what the federal Government is going to do with the federal sales tax.
We know that a federal sales tax can be fair or completely unfair. We also know one additional thing, that is, that people with lower and average incomes will have to spend a larger percentage of their take-home pay on basic goods and commodities. If they are taxed on each and every good which they purchase and each and every service that they use, they will be paying higher taxes to the federal Government than they are at the present time. It will not do them very much good to have a low income tax if, when the second shoe falls, as the expression goes, they end up paying more when the new sales tax measures are introduced. I find it meaningful and scary that we will not know what the Government's plans are with regard to a federal sales tax until after the next election. Here we are on July 21 and the Government is moving quickly with what it calls tax reform because it knows that it is good news for it for the next election. But it will not tell the Canadian people what the total tax bill will be until after that election is finished. I find that basically dishonest. It is certainly advantageous to the Government, but it is basically dishonest in terms of what and how it is telling the people of Canada in terms of what it would do as a government.
I realize that my time is up. I would like to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy):
That the amendment be amended by deleting the word "Corporation" at the end thereof and substituting the following therefor:
"Corporations, and because the Bill fails to ensure that corporations make a fair and regular contribution to federal tax revenues by imposing a minimum corporate tax."
